1.pericope_label: And it came to pass in Iconium, that they went both together into the synagogue of the Jews, and so spake, that a great multitude both of the Jews and also of the Greeks believed.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the timing and the setting. Gill says it came to pass in Iconium when the apostles were got thither, and as soon as they were there, at least the first opportunity they had. Calvin says that in the chapter before, Luke declared how Paul and Barnabas took in hand their embassage unto the Gentiles, and that it might seem to be an unprosperous and unlucky beginning, in that they were not only expelled out of Antioch but also enforced by the obstinate wickedness of certain to shake off the dust from their feet. But though they had but short entertainment in one place, Calvin says, yet do they not yield, because they consider that the Lord had called them upon that condition, that they should do their duty though the whole world and Satan did say nay; therefore we see that they came not only ready to teach, but also armed to enter conflicts, that they might courageously proceed in publishing the gospel even through the midst of combats. That which was once spoken to Jeremiah is common to all the prophets and ministers of God, Calvin adds, they shall fight against thee, but they shall not prevail; and now, whithersoever they fly, they carry with them the same courage still, whereby it appeareth that they were not only furnished for one combat but even for continual warfare. He saith first that they came to Iconium, and therewithal showeth that they sought not there some haven where they might rest quietly, but entered the synagogue as if they had suffered no hurt at all. Calvin refers the Greek phrase rendered both together, forasmuch as it signifieth among the Grecians, rather unto the Jews than unto Paul and Barnabas: therefore I interpret it thus, he says, not that they went in both together, but that they followed the multitude at the solemn and appointed time of the meeting, whence we gather that they spake not secretly with a few men, but in a great assembly of people, whereby they declare their boldness and ready desire, being so far from fearing envy or avoiding danger. As Luke did before show the power of the Spirit in Paul and Barnabas, Calvin says, so now he commendeth another grace of God in that prosperous success which they had: one only sermon which they made was not without fruit, but it brought forth many children of God, as well of the Jews as of the Gentiles. If one, or two, or a few, had believed, they might have thought that they sped well; but the Lord confirmeth them far better, when they gather such plentiful fruit of their doctrine even in a short time, for they knew that so many hearts of men were converted to believe, not so much by their voice as by the power of the Spirit, whereby they might also assure themselves that they themselves were defended by the outstretched hand of God, which did not a little encourage them.

Henry takes the preaching, the pairing and the parity. In these verses, Henry says, we have the preaching of the gospel in Iconium, whither the apostles were forced to retire from Antioch: as the blood of the martyrs has been the seed of the church, so the banishment of the confessors has helped to scatter that seed. They made the first offer of the gospel to the Jews in their synagogues, thither they went, not only as to a place of meeting but as to a place of meeting with them, to whom, wherever they came, they were to apply themselves in the first place. Though the Jews at Antioch had used them barbarously, Henry says, yet they did not therefore decline preaching the gospel to the Jews at Iconium, who perhaps might be better disposed; let not those of any denomination be condemned in the gross, nor some suffer for others' faults, but let us do good to those who have done evil to us. Notice is taken that they went both together into the synagogue, to testify their unanimity and mutual affection, that people might say, See how they love one another, and might think the better of Christianity, and that they might strengthen one another's hands and confirm one another's testimony, and out of the mouth of two witnesses every word might be established: they did not go one one day and another another, nor one go at the beginning and the other some time after, but they went in both together. On the success, Henry says the gospel was now preached to Jews and Gentiles together, and those of each denomination that believed came together into the church: in the close of the foregoing chapter it was preached first to the Jews, and some of them believed, and then to the Gentiles, and some of them believed, but here they are put together, being put upon the same level. The Jews have not so lost their preference as to be thrown behind, Henry says, only the Gentiles are brought to stand upon even terms with them, both are reconciled to God in one body and both together admitted into the church without distinction. There seems to have been something remarkable in the manner of the apostles' preaching here which contributed to their success: they so spoke that a great multitude believed, so plainly, so convincingly, with such an evidence and demonstration of the Spirit and with such power; they so spoke, so warmly, so affectionately, and with such a manifest concern for the souls of men, that one might perceive they were not only convinced, but filled, with the things they spoke of, and that what they spoke came from the heart and therefore was likely to reach to the heart; they so spoke, so earnestly and so seriously, so boldly and courageously, that those who heard them could not but say that God was with them of a truth. Yet the success was not to be attributed to the manner of their preaching, Henry insists, but to the Spirit of God, who made use of that means.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the place, the term Greeks and the grammar. Barnes notes that it was in Iconium that Timothy became acquainted with Paul and his manner of life, and that they spake with such power that their preaching was attended so much with the influence of the Spirit; the Greeks were probably proselytes from the Greeks, who were in the habit of attending the synagogue. Ellicott says the latter term is used in its wider sense, as elsewhere, as equivalent to Gentile, but that it implies that those who were so described spoke and understood Greek; in the former instance these would probably be the proselytes of the gate who heard the Apostles in the synagogue. Robertson notes that the phrase rendered both together is like one used earlier in the book, that the infinitive rendered entered is the subject of the verb it came to pass, and that so spake that is again an infinitive parallel to it. The result clause is an actual result stated with the aorist infinitive believed rather than with the indicative as elsewhere, Robertson says, and adds that it was a tremendous first meeting.

Clarke and Wesley take the power of the speaking. Clarke opens the chapter with a summary of its course, that Paul and Barnabas, having preached at Iconium with great success, are persecuted and obliged to flee to Lystra and Derbe, where they preach and heal a cripple, on which the people, supposing them to be gods, are about to offer them sacrifices and are with difficulty prevented; that certain Jews from Antioch and Iconium, coming thither, induce the people to stone Paul, who, being dragged out of the city as dead while the disciples stand around him, rises up suddenly and returns to the city; and that they afterwards return to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, confirming the disciples and ordaining elders in every Church. On the verse itself Clarke says they so spake with such power and demonstration of the Spirit that a great multitude both of the Jews, genuine descendants of one or other of the twelve tribes, and also of the Greeks, probably such as were proselytes of the gate, believed, received the Christian religion as a revelation from God, and confided in its Author for salvation, according to the apostles' preaching. Wesley says only, they so spake, persecution having increased their strength.

debates: What both together modifies. Henry builds a doctrine of ministerial partnership on it, that they went in together to testify unanimity and to establish every word out of the mouth of two witnesses, insisting they did not go one one day and another another; Calvin refers the Greek phrase to the Jews rather than to the apostles, so that it describes the multitude assembling at the appointed time and says nothing about the two men at all; Robertson notes the phrase and its parallel elsewhere without deciding between them.

What the success is to be credited to. Henry describes the manner of the preaching at length, plain, warm, affectionate, earnest, and then withdraws the credit from it, since the success was not to be attributed to the manner but to the Spirit who made use of that means; Calvin argues the same from the size of the harvest, that so many hearts converted by one sermon shows the power of the Spirit rather than the voice; Barnes and Clarke say only that the preaching was attended with the influence and demonstration of the Spirit.

Who the Greeks were. Ellicott takes the term in its wider sense as equivalent to Gentile, while noting it implies they spoke and understood Greek, and identifies them here with the proselytes of the gate; Barnes agrees that they were probably proselytes in the habit of attending the synagogue; Clarke divides the audience into genuine descendants of the twelve tribes and proselytes of the gate; Henry is interested not in who they were but that Jew and Gentile now stand on even terms.
outliers: Calvin alone reads the chapter as a continuation of a defeat, opening not with Iconium but with the expulsion from Antioch, and finding in it evidence that the apostles were furnished not for one combat but for continual warfare.
Henry alone turns the treatment the apostles received at Antioch into a rule about corporate blame, that none of any denomination should be condemned in the gross nor some suffer for others' faults.
Barnes alone steps outside the scene to note that it was here that Timothy first became acquainted with Paul and his manner of life.
themes: so spake that a great multitude believed
the power of the Spirit in preaching

2.pericope_label: But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles, and made their minds evil affected against the brethren. Long time therefore abode they speaking boldly in the Lord, which gave testimony unto the word of his grace, and granted signs and wonders to be done by their hands.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the stirring up and the use of miracles. Gill says the unbelieving Jews means that part of the Jews which continued in unbelief and rejected the doctrine of the apostles concerning Jesus of Nazareth being the Messiah; these stirred up the Gentiles, who had no knowledge of, nor faith in, this matter. On the next verse Gill says they abode long time at Iconium, undaunted and not discouraged at the treatment they met with. Calvin says they are persecuted now afresh, and that by the Jews, for they were like firebrands to inflame the minds of the Gentiles; it is to be thought that the Gentiles could abide to hear the gospel preached, unless they had been incensed to resist by these fans. He interprets the verb rendered made evil affected as to infect with a malicious affection, or to enforce to do hurt. Under the name brethren, Calvin says, Luke comprehendeth, in my judgment, all the godly, to wit, that they were vexed and troubled whosoever embraced the gospel, as if some pernicious sect had risen to spread discord, to trouble the peace of the city, to shake the public state; yet if any had rather restrain it unto Paul and Barnabas, I am not greatly against him. On the next verse Calvin says Luke declareth that Paul and Barnabas did not depart the city so soon as they saw some set against them, for when he saith that they behaved themselves boldly he giveth us an inkling that there was cause of fear offered them; whence we gather that they stood stoutly, and that through rare constancy and courage they counted all dangers as nothing until they were compelled by violence to depart. The phrase in the Lord may be expounded diversely, Calvin says, either that they behaved themselves stoutly in the Lord's cause, or that they trusted to his grace and were thereby encouraged; I have followed that which was more common, that they behaved themselves freely and boldly in the Lord, that is, being holpen not by their own strength but by his grace. He showeth immediately after after what sort they were encouraged in the Lord, to wit, because he approveth the doctrine by signs and miracles: seeing that they knew thereby that the Lord was present with them, and that his hand was nigh to help them, they were worthily pricked forward to behave themselves stoutly. We must note this phrase, that the Lord gave witness to the gospel in miracles, Calvin says, for it showeth the true use of miracles. This is the first end, that they may show to us the power and grace of God; but because we be wrong and perverse interpreters of them, lest they be drawn unto abuse and corruption, God doth never suffer them to be separated from his word. For if miracles were wrought at any time without his word, first, that was very seldom, and secondly, there came but small fruit thereof; and God hath wrought miracles for the most part whereby the world might know him not simply, or in his bare majesty, but in his word. So Luke saith that the gospel was established by miracles, not that some confused religion might possess the minds of men, but that Paul's doctrine going before, they might be brought unto the pure worship of God. Whence we may easily gather how foolishly the Papists deal, Calvin says, when they endeavour to lead away the world from the reverence of God and the gospel by bare miracles; for we must hold that principle, that those miracles which came from God at any time did never tend to any other end but that the gospel might have its perfect and full authority. Now must we see whether the gospel command us to call upon the dead, to burn incense to idols, to translate unto feigned saints the grace of Christ, to take in hand vowed pilgrimages, to invent profane worshippings whereof there is no mention made in the Word of God; but there is nothing more contrary to the gospel than that these superstitions should take place. To the same end tendeth that which Luke saith, that the Lord granted that by the hands of his servants miracles might be done, in which words he teacheth that those were only ministers who obeyed God, and that he was the author, who used their hand and industry; wherefore, in speaking properly, we cannot say that they were Paul and Barnabas's miracles, but the miracles of God alone, who doth so work by men that he will not have his glory darkened by their ministry. We must note the title of the gospel which Luke putteth in here, Calvin adds, that it may be made to us more amiable; for in calling it the word of grace it hath a most pleasant taste, because salvation is offered to the world in it through Christ, and we must understand the contrariety with the law, wherein only the curse is set before us.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the source of the persecution, the length of the stay and the grammar. Barnes says made their minds evil affected means irritated or exasperated them, and that against the brethren uses one of the common appellations by which Christians were known. On the next verse he says that in this city they were not daunted by persecution: it seems probable that there were here no forcible or public measures to expel them, as there had been at Antioch, and they therefore regarded it as their duty to remain, while God granted them here also great success, which was the main reason for their continuing a long time. Persecution and opposition may be attended often with signal success to the gospel, Barnes adds. Speaking boldly in the Lord means in the cause of the Lord Jesus, or in his name and authority, and perhaps the expression includes the idea of their trusting in the Lord; which gave testimony means that he bore witness to the truth of their message by working miracles. This was evidently the Lord Jesus to whom reference is made, Barnes says, and it shows that he was still, though bodily absent from them, clothed with power, and still displayed that power in the advancement of his cause; the conversion of sinners accomplished by him is always a testimony as decided as it is cheering to the labours of his servants. The word of his grace means his gracious word or message, and signs and wonders means miracles. Ellicott says it is the distinguishing feature of nearly all the persecutions in the Acts that they originated in the hostility of the Jews: the case of Demetrius furnishes almost the only exception, and even there the Jews apparently fomented the enmity of the Greek craftsmen, and so at a considerably later date, in the year 169, we find them prominent in bringing about the persecution which ended in the death of Polycarp at Smyrna. On the next verse Ellicott says long time abode they can hardly be understood as involving a stay of less than several months, during which Paul and Barnabas, as before, were working for their livelihood; the boldness consisted, as the context shows, in a full declaration of the gospel of the grace of God as contrasted with the narrowing Judaism with which the Greek proselytes had previously been familiar. It will be noted that here also, as so often elsewhere, the miracles that were wrought came as the confirmation of faith, not as its foundation. Robertson notes that the participle rendered that were disobedient is a first aorist active articular participle, not the present as the Textus Receptus has it, but that the meaning is probably the Jews that disbelieved rather than that disobeyed: strictly one verb does mean to disobey and another to disbelieve, but that distinction is not observed in John or elsewhere in Acts, since the word means to be unwilling to be persuaded, to withhold belief and then also to withhold obedience, and the two meanings run into one another, for to disbelieve the word of God is to disobey God. Made them evil affected is the first aorist of an old verb meaning to do evil to, to ill-treat, and then in later Greek as here to embitter, to exasperate, in that sense only here in the New Testament. Evidently Paul preached the same message as in Antioch, Robertson says, for it won both Jews and Gentiles and displeased the rabbis, and Codex Bezae adds here that the chiefs of the synagogue and the rulers brought persecution upon Paul and Barnabas, just as was argued about Antioch; outside the synagogue the Jews would poison the minds of the Gentiles against them. He quotes the suggestion that the story of Thecla suggests a means, and that perhaps the apostles were brought before the magistrates on some charge of interference with family life, the magistrates however must have seen at once that there was no legal case against them, and by a sentence of acquittal or in some other way the Lord gave peace. As we have it, Robertson says, the story of Paul and Thecla undoubtedly has apocryphal features, though Thecla may very well be an historical character here at Iconium where the story is located; certainly the picture of Paul therein drawn cannot be considered authentic though a true tradition may underlie it, namely bald, bowlegged, strongly built, small in stature, with large eyes and meeting eyebrows and longish nose, full of grace, sometimes looking like a man, sometimes having the face of an angel. On the next verse Robertson notes an accusative of duration of time, possibly six months, and an antithesis in the following verses; after the persecution and vindication there was a season of great opportunity which Paul and Barnabas used to the full, speaking boldly in the Lord, upon the basis of the Lord Jesus, and the Lord Jesus bore witness to the word of his grace as he always does, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands, the present participle and present infinitive marking repetition of both signs and wonders just as had happened with Peter and John and the other apostles. The time of peace could not last forever with such a work of grace as this, Robertson says: a second explosion of persecution was bound to come, and some manuscripts actually have the words a second time.

Clarke takes the Gentiles, the boldness and the grant of miracles. Stirred up the Gentiles means such as were mere heathens, Clarke says, and thus distinguished from the Jews and the Greeks who were proselytes; evil affected means irritated or exasperated their minds against the brethren, the disciples of Christ, one of their appellations before they were called Christians at Antioch. On the next verse Clarke says that because they had great success they continued a long time, gaining many converts and building up those who had believed in their most holy faith, notwithstanding the opposition they met with both from the unbelieving Jews and heathens. Speaking boldly means having great liberty of speech, a copious and commanding eloquence springing from a consciousness of the truth which they preached; the word of his grace is the Gospel of Jesus Christ, which is the doctrine of God's grace, mercy or favour to mankind. And granted signs and wonders to be done, Clarke says, for no apostle could work a miracle by himself, nor was any sign or wonder wrought even by the greatest apostle but by an especial grant or dispensation of God: this power was not resident in them at all times, it was only now and then communicated, when a miracle was necessary for the confirmation of the truth preached.

debates: Whether the participle means disbelieved or disobeyed. Robertson corrects the text to the aorist, judges the sense to be disbelieved, and then argues that the distinction collapses, since to be unwilling to be persuaded is to withhold belief and then obedience alike; Gill takes it simply as those who continued in unbelief; Calvin does not raise the question.

Who the brethren are. Barnes and Clarke take the word as a standing name for the disciples before the name Christian was given at Antioch; Calvin extends it to all the godly, so that every convert was harassed as a member of a sect thought to shake the public state, and then concedes that he is not greatly against restraining it to Paul and Barnabas.

What the miracles were for. Ellicott says they came as the confirmation of faith and not as its foundation; Calvin says God never suffers them to be separated from his word, since without it they were seldom wrought and bore small fruit, and turns the point into an attack on those who would draw the world away from the gospel by bare miracles; Clarke says the power was not resident in the apostles but granted when a miracle was needed to confirm the preaching; Barnes reads the testimony as borne by the Lord Jesus himself, bodily absent yet still clothed with power.

How long the long time was. Ellicott will not allow less than several months and has the two working for their livelihood through them; Robertson reads an accusative of duration and guesses six months, adding that such a season could not last and that some manuscripts record the next outbreak as a second time; Clarke explains the length by the success rather than measuring it.
outliers: Robertson alone leaves the canonical text for the apocryphal Acts of Paul and Thecla, using it to guess at the legal charge behind the persecution and quoting its portrait of Paul as bald, bowlegged and small in stature, with meeting eyebrows and the face of an angel.

Calvin alone turns the clause about signs and wonders into a polemic, arguing from the rule that miracles are never separated from the word to a list of practices he says the gospel nowhere commands: calling on the dead, burning incense to idols, and vowed pilgrimages.

Ellicott alone reaches forward out of the first century to a second-century martyrdom, citing the death of Polycarp as evidence that the pattern of Jewish instigation persisted long after Acts closes.
themes: the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles
minds evil affected against the brethren
signs and wonders by their hands

4.pericope_label: But the multitude of the city was divided: and part held with the Jews, and part with the apostles. And when there was an assault made both of the Gentiles, and also of the Jews with their rulers, to use them despitefully, and to stone them,

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the division and the flight. Gill says the multitude of the city was divided in their sentiments about the apostles, their doctrines and miracles, some approving them, others condemning their doctrines as false and their miracles as delusions. On the next verse he glosses the assault as a strong bias and inclination in the minds. Calvin says the most troublesome part of the tragedy followeth now, for the city is divided into two parts, and at length Paul and Barnabas, being enforced by the uproar of the people, depart unto another place. If it be demanded what was the original of the discord, Calvin says, assuredly it flowed from the gospel, to which notwithstanding there is nothing more contrary than to cause discord; but the forwardness of men causeth that the gospel, which ought to be the bond of unity, is, so soon as it cometh abroad, the occasion of tumults. Wherefore, so soon as any schism ariseth, before we condemn those who seem to be the authors, it behoveth us wisely to consider who ought to bear the blame. We hear here that one city was divided, whereby some were brought unto Christ, and the Spirit of God pronounceth this to the praise, and not the shame, of Paul and Barnabas; the same rule must we observe at this day, lest the gospel be burdened with false envy, if it bring not men together unto God, but the wicked rage against it. It is assuredly a miserable matter to see division among men, Calvin says, but as the unity is accursed which doth separate us all from God, so it were better that a few should depart an hundred times from all the whole world, and in the mean season come in favour again with God, than that, disagreeing with him continually, they should have peace with the world. On the next verse Calvin says, mark how far forth the holy champions of Christ did suffer: they give not back when their enemies do only set themselves against them, but when the sedition waxeth hot and they be in danger of stoning, though they have many favourers of their doctrine, they go no further, but remembering the saying of Christ wherein he warneth the faithful in patience to possess their souls, they avoid the fury of the enemy. And though they fly, lest they throw themselves headlong into death, yet their constancy in preaching the gospel doth sufficiently declare that they feared not danger, for Luke saith that they preached the gospel in other places also. This is the right kind of fear, Calvin says, when the servants of Christ do not run wilfully into the hands of their enemies, of them to be murdered, and yet they do not abandon their duty; neither doth fear hinder them from obeying God when he calleth, and so consequently they can afford, if need be, to go even through death itself to do their duty.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the schism, the rulers and the word apostles. Barnes says the multitude was divided into parties, the Greek being that there was a schism, and that part held to the doctrines of the Jews in opposition to the apostles. A revival of religion may produce excitement by the bad passions of opposers, Barnes says; the enemies of the truth may form parties and organize opposition, and it is no uncommon thing even now for such parties to be formed, but the fault is not in Christianity: it lies with those who form a party against religion and who confederate themselves, as was done here, to oppose it. On the next verse Barnes says an assault made is in the Greek a rush, denoting an impetuous excitement and aggression, a rush to put them to death; it rather describes a popular tumult than a calm and deliberate purpose, and there was a violent, tumultuous excitement. To use them despitefully means to reproach them, to bring contempt upon them, to injure them; to stone them means to put them to death by stoning, probably as blasphemers. Ellicott says the context shows that Luke writes of the bulk of the heathen population: no numbers are given, but we may fairly assume that the converts were in a minority, and that they belonged as a rule to the lower classes, and that the chief men and women of the city, as at the Pisidian Antioch, were against them. The rulers who are named would seem, from the form of punishment selected, to have been those of the Jewish synagogue, Ellicott says, and the crime of which the preachers were accused, as in the case of Stephen, to have been blasphemy. On the next verse he says the verb rendered to use them despitefully expresses wanton insult and outrage, that Paul uses the noun derived from it to express the character of his own conduct as a persecutor, and must have felt, as afterwards in the actual stoning later in this chapter, that he was receiving the just reward of his own deeds. Robertson notes that the verb rendered was divided is the first aorist passive of an old verb to split, to make a schism or factions as Sadducees and Pharisees, and that this division was within the Gentile populace; part held is literally some were with the Jews, part with the apostles, a common demonstrative of contrast. The Jewish leaders made some impression on the Gentiles as at Antioch in Pisidia and later at Thessalonica, he says. This is the first time in the Acts that Paul and Barnabas are termed apostles, Robertson notes, and elsewhere in the Acts the word is restricted to the twelve; certainly Luke does not here employ it in that technical sense, since to have followed Jesus in his ministry and to have seen the Risen Christ was essential to the technical use. Whether Barnabas had seen the Risen Christ we do not know, but certainly Paul had, and Paul claimed to be an apostle on a par with the twelve. The word originally means simply one sent, like messengers of the churches with the collection, and the Jews used it of those sent from Jerusalem to collect the temple tribute; Paul applies the word to James the Lord's brother, to Epaphroditus as the messenger of the church in Philippi, to Silvanus and Timothy, apparently to Apollos, and to Andronicus and Junias, and he even calls the Judaizers false apostles. On the next verse Robertson says an onset is a rush or impulse, an old word but only twice in the New Testament, and it probably denotes not an actual attack so much as the open start, the co-operation of both Jews and Gentiles, the disaffected portion, with their rulers, that is the rulers of the Jewish synagogue. The city officials would hardly join in a mob like this, Robertson says, though two commentators think that the city magistrates were also involved as in Antioch in Pisidia. To entreat them shamefully is the first aorist active infinitive of an old verb to insult insolently, and to stone is from a late verb meaning to pelt with stones, the verb used of the stoning of Stephen. The plan to stone them shows that the Jews were in the lead and followed by the Gentile rabble, he says, and quotes that legal proceedings having failed, the only resource left for the Jews was illegal violence.

Clarke takes the division and the assault. The multitude of the city was divided, Clarke says: the Jews treated the apostles as false teachers and their miracles as impositions, and many of the people held with them, while the others, who had not hardened their hearts against the truth, felt the force of it, and being without prejudice could easily discern the miracles to be the work of God, and therefore held with the apostles. On the next verse Clarke says an assault made means that a desperate attempt was made by their rulers, that is by the heathen rulers of the people and the rulers of the synagogue; to use them despitefully means to expose them, bring them into contempt, and make them appear as monsters or movers of sedition, and then to stone them for this falsely alleged crime.

debates: Who the rulers were. Robertson keeps them to the synagogue, on the ground that the city officials would hardly join in a mob like this, while reporting that two commentators think the magistrates were involved as at Pisidian Antioch; Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from the form of punishment selected, stoning being the penalty for blasphemy as in the case of Stephen; Clarke will not choose, and reads the phrase as covering both the heathen rulers of the people and the rulers of the synagogue.

Where the blame for the division lies. Barnes says the fault is not in Christianity but in those who confederate against it; Calvin grants that the discord flowed from the gospel and turns it into a rule of judgment, that before condemning the apparent authors of a schism we must consider who ought to bear the blame; Clarke divides the population by disposition, the hardened against the unprejudiced.

Whether apostles is used in its technical sense. Robertson says it cannot be, since this is the first time in Acts that Paul and Barnabas bear the title and the book elsewhere restricts it to the twelve, then traces the wider use through Paul's own letters; the others take the word as it stands and comment on the division rather than the title.

How violent the assault already was. Barnes reads the Greek as a rush denoting impetuous excitement and aggression, a violent tumultuous purpose to put them to death; Robertson thinks it denotes not the attack itself so much as the open start of it; Gill reduces it to a strong bias and inclination in the minds.
outliers: Robertson alone turns one word of the verse into an excursus on apostleship, canvassing whether Barnabas had seen the Risen Christ and cataloguing everyone Paul calls an apostle, down to Epaphroditus, Andronicus and Junias, and the Judaizers he calls false apostles.

Ellicott alone reads Paul's own persecuting past into the verb, noting that the noun formed from it is the word Paul uses of himself as a persecutor, and that in the stoning a few verses later he must have felt he was receiving the just reward of his own deeds.

Calvin alone prefers a division to a peace, arguing that since the unity which separates us all from God is accursed, it were better that a few should depart an hundred times from the whole world than keep peace with it while disagreeing with God.
themes: the multitude of the city was divided
the first use of apostles for Paul and Barnabas
an assault made with their rulers

6.pericope_label: They were ware of it, and fled unto Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and unto the region that lieth round about: and there they preached the gospel.

schools.summary: Gill takes the deliberation and the later history. They were ware of it, Gill says, means they understood it, were apprised of it, and well weighed it, and considered it in their minds, and what was best to be done at this juncture. On the next verse he says they did not sit still nor hide themselves in these places, but preached the Gospel, the good news and glad tidings of the incarnation of Christ, of redemption, peace and pardon through his blood, justification by his righteousness, and spiritual and eternal salvation through him. In one very ancient printed copy and in another, and in the Greek copies still current centuries later, Gill notes, these words are added: and the whole multitude were moved at their doctrines, and Paul and Barnabas continued at Lystra, which agrees with what follows. It is very likely that many were converted in each of these cities and in the adjacent country, and that churches were raised in these places, Gill says; this seems manifest from Artemas, who is said to be one of the seventy disciples and is reported to be bishop of Lystra, though we meet with nothing in ecclesiastical history concerning the churches in either of these places until the sixth century, when at the fifth Roman synod there were present the bishops of Lystra and Derbe.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the flight, the geography and the province. Barnes says they were in some way informed of the excitement and of their danger, and fled unto Lystra, a city of Lycaonia a few miles south of Iconium; Derbe was a short distance east of Lystra. Lycaonia was one of the provinces of Asia Minor, having Galatia north, Pisidia south, Cappadocia east and Phrygia west; it was formerly within the limits of Phrygia but was erected into a separate province by Augustus. The region round about means the adjacent country, Barnes says, and though persecuted they still preached, and though driven from one city they fled into another: this was the direction of the Saviour. Ellicott says that here again we can scarcely fail to trace a literal obedience to our Lord's commands. The direction of the apostles' journey now took them into a wilder and less civilised region, he says: the range of the Taurus cut it off from the more cultivated country of Cilicia and Pisidia, and it is described as a dreary plain, bare of trees, destitute of fresh water, and with several salt lakes. Ellicott quotes Ovid, speaking of it as the result of personal observation, that where men once dwelt a marshy lake is seen, and coots and bitterns haunt the waters green. The very name Lycaonia, interpreted traditionally as Wolf-land, the local legend deriving it from Lycaon who had been transformed into a wolf, represented but too faithfully the character of the inhabitants. The travellers were also losing the protection which a Roman citizen might claim in a Roman province, Ellicott says, Lycaonia, which had been annexed in the year 17 to the Roman province of Galatia, having been assigned by Caligula to Antiochus, King of Commagene. So wild a country was hardly likely to attract Jewish settlers, and there is no trace in Luke's narrative of the existence of a synagogue in either of the two cities; for the first time, so far as we know, Paul had to begin his work by preaching to the heathen. Of the two towns named, Ellicott says, Lystra was about forty miles to the south-east of Iconium, Derbe about twenty miles further to the east; the former, which lies to the north of a lofty conical mountain called the Black Mountain, is now known as the thousand and one churches, from the ruins that abound there. The addition of the region that lieth round about suggests that the cities were not large enough to supply a sufficient field of action, and the work in the country villages must obviously, even more than in the cities, have been entirely among the Gentiles; among the converts of this region, and probably of this time, we may note Timotheus of Lystra and Gaius of Derbe. Robertson notes that they became aware of it is the second aorist active participle of an old word to see together, to become conscious of, in the New Testament only in Luke and Paul, and that fled is the second aorist of an old verb found in the New Testament only here and in Hebrews. Paul and Barnabas had no idea of remaining to be stoned by this mob, Robertson says: it is a wise preacher who always knows when to stand his ground and when to leave for the glory of God, and they were following the directions of the Lord Jesus given to the twelve on their special tour of Galilee. Lystra and Derbe were cities of Lycaonia still part of the Province of Galatia, though in another region, not far from the base of the Black Mountain; a scholar has apparently identified Lystra by an inscription about eighteen miles south-southwest from Iconium near a village, and Derbe probably near another village, though its location is really not known. Lystra had been made a colony in the year 6 before Christ, Robertson says, and Derbe was the frontier city of the Roman empire in the south-east; these are the only cities mentioned, but they were of importance and show that Paul kept to his plan of going to centres of influence, and the new imperial road from Antioch and Iconium reached these cities. The region round about was a high table land, ill-watered, bleak, but suited for sheep pasture. On the next verse Robertson notes a periphrastic imperfect middle, and says we are to think of extensive evangelistic work perhaps with the assistance of disciples from Antioch and Iconium, since Paul and Barnabas could not speak Lycaonian.

Clarke takes the flight and the puzzle about Iconium. They were ware of it means they were informed of the scheme and of the attempt that was about to be made, Clarke says, and fled unto Lystra and Derbe; they did not leave the province of Lycaonia, but went to other towns and cities. Lystra lay to the south and Derbe to the north of Iconium, according to the general opinion. Strabo tells us expressly that Iconium was within Lycaonia, Clarke notes, saying that thence are the Lycaonian hills, plain, cold, naked, and pastures for wild asses, and that about these places stands Iconium, a town built in a better soil; Ptolemy also places Iconium in Lycaonia. How comes it, then, Clarke asks, that Luke does not call Iconium a city of Lycaonia as well as Derbe and Lystra? Pliny solves this difficulty, Clarke says, by stating that there was granted a tetrarchy out of Lycaonia, on that side which borders upon Galatia, consisting of fourteen cities, the most famous of which is Iconium. On the next verse Clarke says that wherever they went they were always employed in their Master's work, and that some manuscripts of considerable note add here, and all the people were moved at their preaching, but Paul and Barnabas tarried at Lystra.

debates: Where Lystra and Derbe lie. Clarke puts Lystra south and Derbe north of Iconium on the general opinion of his day; Barnes puts Lystra a few miles south and Derbe a short distance east of Lystra; Ellicott stretches the same journey to forty miles south-east and twenty miles further east; Robertson has an inscription that fixes Lystra some eighteen miles south-southwest of Iconium and concedes that the site of Derbe is really not known. A century of survey work separates the first answer from the last.

What legal ground they had come onto. Ellicott says they were losing the protection a Roman citizen might claim, Lycaonia having been assigned away from the province of Galatia to a client king; Robertson says the two cities were still part of the Province of Galatia, that Lystra had been made a colony and Derbe was the frontier city of the empire in the south-east, and that the new imperial road reached them both.

Why Luke does not call Iconium a city of Lycaonia. Clarke raises the difficulty against two ancient geographers who place Iconium inside Lycaonia, and resolves it from a third, who records that a tetrarchy of fourteen cities was cut out of Lycaonia on the Galatian side, Iconium being the most famous of them; the others pass the wording without remark.

What the Western addition at the end of the verse is worth. Gill reports it from two early printed copies and says the words stood in the Greek copies centuries after; Clarke reports the same words from manuscripts of considerable note; neither rejects it, and Gill observes that it agrees with what follows.
outliers: Ellicott alone presses the name of the province into a character sketch, taking Lycaonia as Wolf-land from the legend of a man turned into a wolf and saying the name represented but too faithfully the character of the inhabitants, and quoting a Roman poet who had seen the marshes for himself.

Robertson alone raises the language barrier, observing that the work must have been carried on with the help of disciples from Antioch and Iconium, since neither Paul nor Barnabas could speak Lycaonian.

Gill alone follows the two towns forward out of the New Testament, noting that no church in either is heard of in ecclesiastical history until the sixth century, when their bishops appear at a Roman synod.
themes: the region that lieth round about

8.pericope_label: And there sat a certain man at Lystra, impotent in his feet, being a cripple from his mother's womb, who never had walked: the same heard Paul speak: who stedfastly beholding him, and perceiving that he had faith to be healed,

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the posture, the hearing and the nature of the faith. Gill says there sat a certain man at Lystra where the apostle was preaching, and perhaps he sat there to beg, where there was a great concourse of people, and which might be in the open street. On the next verse Gill says the same heard Paul speak, that is, preach the Gospel; he was one of his hearers, and faith came to him by hearing, and the Arabic version adds that he cried unto Paul, whom he heard. Calvin says Luke reciteth one miracle which we may think was one of many, but there was mention made of it alone by reason of the famous event, for we shall see by and by what happened. Luke reckoneth up the circumstances which do more plainly set forth the power of God, Calvin says, when he saith that the man did never walk, and that he was a cripple even from his mother's womb, and that he was suddenly healed by the voice of Paul alone before the eyes of all men, and that his legs, which were dead, were made nimble, so that he leapt up without making any stop. On the next verse Calvin says hearing is set down first, that we may know that the faith which Luke will commend by and by was conceived of Paul's doctrine; therefore, when he heard Paul, he hoped to be healed. But the question is whether this was promised to him specially, Calvin says, for God doth not command us to hope for everything forthwith when he offereth unto us eternal salvation in the gospel. I answer, that this was a singular and extraordinary motion of the Spirit of God in the cripple, as it was on the other side in Paul, when he knew his faith by beholding him only. It may be that many may receive the gospel and yet they shall not be cured of those diseases wherewith they are vexed; but forasmuch as God was determined to show a token of his grace in the cripple, he prepared his mind before, and made him capable of this that should come upon him. Wherefore we must not make this a common rule, Calvin insists, because the cripple believed that he should be healed, but it was a peculiar preparation to receive the gift of healing; and this kind of faith is likewise particular which giveth room for miracles, which many of God's children do want, who are notwithstanding endued with the Spirit of adoption. We know how doubtful and how deceitful a thing the countenance of man is, Calvin says, therefore there could no sure judgment be given thereby of faith, which hath God alone to be witness thereof; but the cripple's faith was revealed to Paul by the secret inspiration of the Spirit, as he was to the apostles their only guide and master to work miracles.

Henry takes the parallel, the case and the expectation. In these verses we have a miraculous cure wrought by Paul at Lystra upon a cripple that had been lame from his birth, Henry says, such a one as was miraculously cured by Peter and John: that introduced the gospel among the Jews, this among the Gentiles, and both that and this were designed to represent the impotency of all the children of men in spiritual things, for they are lame from their birth till the grace of God puts strength into them, since it was when we were yet without strength that Christ died for the ungodly. Observe the deplorable case of the poor cripple, Henry says: he was impotent in his feet, disabled to such a degree that it was impossible he should set his foot to the ground to lay any stress upon it, and it was well known that he had been so from his mother's womb and that he never had walked nor could stand up. We should take occasion hence to thank God for the use of our limbs, Henry says, and those who are deprived of it may observe that their case is not singular. Then observe the expectation that was raised in him of a cure: he heard Paul preach, and it is likely was much affected with what he heard, believed that the messengers, having their commission thence, had a divine power going along with them, and were therefore able to cure him of his lameness. This Paul was aware of, by the spirit of discerning that he had, and perhaps the aspect of his countenance did in part witness for him: Paul perceived that he had faith to be healed, desired it, hoped for it, had such a thing in his thoughts, which it does not appear that the lame man Peter healed had, for he expected no more than an alms; there was not found such great faith in Israel as was among the Gentiles. Paul, perceiving that he had faith to be healed, brought the word and healed him, Henry says, and God will not disappoint the desires that are of his own kindling, nor the hopes of his own raising. Paul spoke to him with a loud voice, either because he was at some distance, or to show that the true miracles wrought by the power of Christ were far unlike the lying wonders wrought by deceivers, that peeped and muttered and whispered; God saith, I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth. Paul spoke with a loud voice that the people about might take notice and have their expectations raised of the effect. It does not appear that this cripple was a beggar, Henry says: it is said that he sat, not that he sat begging; but we may imagine how melancholy it was to him to see other people walking about him and himself disabled, and therefore how welcome Paul's word was to him, stand upright on thy feet, help thyself and God shall help thee, try whether thou hast strength and thou shalt find that thou hast. Some copies read it, I say unto thee, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, stand upright on thy feet.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the posture, the record of the infirmity and the gaze. Barnes says there sat means there dwelt, but that the word sat indicates his usual posture, his helpless condition, such persons commonly sitting at the wayside or in some public place to ask for alms. Impotent in his feet means without any power, entirely deprived of the use of his feet; who never had walked means that the miracle would be the more remarkable, as the man would be well known and there could be no plea that there was an imposition. As they were persecuted from place to place and opposed in every manner, Barnes says, it was desirable that a signal miracle should be performed to carry forward and establish the work of the gospel. On the next verse he says stedfastly beholding him means fixing his eyes intently on him, and that how Paul perceived his faith is not said: perhaps it was indicated by the ardour, humility and strong desire depicted in his countenance, for he had heard Paul, and perhaps the apostle had dwelt particularly on the miracles with which the gospel had been attested, and the miracles wrought in Iconium had doubtless also been heard of in Lystra. Ellicott notes, as in two earlier passages, the characteristic care to record the duration of the infirmity which was supernaturally cured. On the next verse he notes once more the recurrence of the characteristic word and look, and says that here, as so often, as if it were the general though not the universal law of miraculous working, faith is pre-supposed as the condition. It follows from this, no less than from the tense of the verb, used to listen to Paul as he spoke, that he had for some days been among Paul's hearers, had heard the gospel of the death and resurrection of Jesus, and had found that such a Saviour met his every need; all this the Apostle read, with that earnest gaze of his, in the man's upward look. Robertson notes that the name of the town is neuter plural here and feminine singular elsewhere, that there was apparently no synagogue in Lystra and so not many Jews, and that Paul and Barnabas had to do open-air preaching and probably had difficulty in being understood by the natives, though both Greek and Latin inscriptions were discovered there. The incident narrated here shows how they got a real hearing among these rude heathen, he says. There sat is the imperfect middle, was sitting, and this case is very much like the one healed by Peter, possibly outside the gate or in some public place. Impotent in his feet is an old verbal, only here in the New Testament in this sense, common in medical writers in the sense of impotent; and the best manuscripts read walked, a first aorist, not had walked. On the next verse Robertson says the same is just this one, and heard is an imperfect, was listening to Paul speaking, either at the gate or in the market place, Paul preaching to such as would listen or could understand his Greek; a scholar thinks that the cripple was a proselyte, and at any rate he may have heard of the miracles wrought at Iconium, and Paul may have spoken of the work of healing wrought by Jesus. This man was no mendicant pretender, Robertson says, for his history was known from his birth. Fastening his eyes upon him is the same participle used earlier of Paul, and Paul saw a new hope in the man's eyes and face; he had faith is a present indicative retained in indirect discourse, and to be made whole is from a verb meaning to make sound and also to save, here clearly to make whole or well.

Clarke and Wesley take the diagnosis and the faith. Impotent in his feet means he had no muscular power, Clarke says, and probably his ankle bones were dislocated, or he had what is commonly termed club feet; this is the more likely, as he is said to have been lame from his mother's womb and to have never walked. On the next verse Clarke asks how this faith came to this poor heathen, and answers, by hearing the word of God preached, for it is said the same heard Paul speak; it appears that he credited the doctrine he heard and believed that Jesus could, if he would, make him whole, and besides, he must have heard of the miracles which the apostles had wrought, and this would raise his expectation of receiving a cure. Wesley says he had faith to be healed, for he felt the power of God in his soul, and thence knew it was sufficient to heal his body also.

debates: Whether the man was begging. Gill supposes he sat there to beg where there was a great concourse of people, and Barnes says the word indicates the usual posture of such persons, who sat by the wayside to ask alms; Henry refuses the inference, that it is said he sat, not that he sat begging; Robertson agrees, calling him no mendicant pretender since his history was known from his birth.

How Paul perceived the man's faith. Barnes says it is not stated and guesses the ardour and strong desire depicted in his countenance; Ellicott has the Apostle read it in the man's upward look with that earnest gaze of his; Robertson says Paul saw a new hope in his eyes and face; Calvin denies that any sure judgment of faith can be given by so deceitful a thing as the countenance of man, and refers the knowledge instead to the secret inspiration of the Spirit.

Whether the case makes a rule. Calvin insists that we must not make a common rule of it, since this was a singular motion of the Spirit and many receive the gospel who are not cured of the diseases that vex them, this kind of faith being one that many of God's children want; Ellicott calls faith the general though not the universal law of miraculous working; Henry sets no limit, saying God will not disappoint the desires that are of his own kindling.

What made the man expect a cure. Clarke and Gill trace it to the preaching he had heard; Ellicott presses the tense of the verb to show he had been listening for some days and had heard the gospel of the death and resurrection; Robertson reports the suggestion that he was a proselyte and adds the report of the miracles at Iconium; Wesley traces it inward, to the power of God he felt in his soul.
outliers: Clarke alone attempts a physical diagnosis, offering dislocated ankle bones or what is commonly termed club feet as the likelier explanation of a lameness from birth.

Henry alone accounts for the loud voice, either because Paul stood at some distance or to distinguish true miracles from the lying wonders of deceivers who peeped and muttered and whispered, since God has said he did not speak in secret in a dark place of the earth.

Robertson alone notes that the preaching at Lystra was open-air and probably hard for the natives to follow, and that the whole incident shows how two men without a synagogue got a real hearing among rude heathen.
themes: a cripple from his mother’s womb
faith as the condition of healing

10.pericope_label: Said with a loud voice, Stand upright on thy feet. And he leaped and walked. And when the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the voice, the leap and the idolatry. Gill says the loud voice was used not only that the man, but that all, might hear and attend to the miracle about to be wrought. On the next verse he says the people saw what Paul had done in curing the lame man in so marvellous a manner, and concluded it to be a divine work, and what a mere creature could never perform. Calvin notes that many old books, and those of great credit, add the words, I say to thee in the name of Jesus Christ, and surely we see how careful the apostles were to magnify the name of Christ in all miracles; therefore I think that that was expressed by Luke, and yet we cannot find it commonly now in the printed books. Whereas Luke saith afterward that the lame man leapt up, Calvin says, it serveth not only for the commendation of God's power, but also such readiness and willingness to obey did testify that he was rightly prepared by the Lord, so that he did already walk in mind when his feet were as yet dead; although his speed in rising made the power of God more manifest, to which end also Paul exalted his voice, that the sudden change might the more move the multitude. On the next verse Calvin says this history doth abundantly testify how ready and bent men are unto vanity: Paul uttered not that word abruptly, but he added it as it were a conclusion to the sermon made concerning Christ, yet the people ascribe the praise of the miracle unto their idols, as if they had heard no word of Christ. It is no such wonder that barbarous men fell unto superstition which they had imbibed from their childhood so soon as they saw the miracle, Calvin says, but this vice is too common everywhere, and it is so bred in us to be perverse and wrong interpreters of the works of God; hence come such gross dotings of superstitions, because catching rashly at miracles they take no heed to doctrine. For which cause we must take the better heed, and be the more sober, lest we happen with the sense of the flesh to corrupt the power of God which shineth and appeareth to us for our salvation; and no marvel if the Lord would have only a few miracles wrought, and that for a short time, lest through the lust of men they should be drawn unto a far contrary end, because it is unmeet that he should set his name to be mocked of the world. This was an opinion drawn from old fables, Calvin says, which notwithstanding took their beginning of truth: the books of the poets are full of these toys, that the gods were often seen upon earth in the likeness of men, and yet we may well think that this came not of nothing, but rather that profane men did turn that into fables which the holy fathers taught in times past concerning angels; and it may be that Satan, when he had men besotted, did with diverse jugglings delude them. Whatsoever was God's, whensoever it went over to the infidels, was corrupted by their wicked inventions, and the same must we think of sacrifices. When the men of Lycaonia see unwonted power in the cripple that was healed, they persuade themselves that it is a work of God, and this is all well, Calvin says; but it was evil done in that they forge to themselves false gods in Paul and Barnabas, according to the old error. For what is the cause that they prefer Barnabas before Paul, save only because they follow the childish surmise concerning Mercury, the interpreter of the gods, in which they had been nourished? By which example we are taught what a mischief it is to be accustomed and acquainted with errors in youth, Calvin says, which can so hardly be rooted out of the mind that even through the works of God, whereby they ought to have been redressed, they wax more hard.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the leap, the language and the legend. Barnes refers the loud voice and the leaping to earlier scenes in the gospel and in the third chapter of this book. On the next verse he says they lifted up their voices, speaking with astonishment such as might be expected when it was supposed that the gods had come down. What the speech of Lycaonia was has much puzzled commentators, Barnes says: it was probably a mixture of the Greek and Syriac, since in that region generally the Greek was usually spoken with more or less purity, and from the fact that it was not far from the regions of Syria it is probable that the Greek language was corrupted with this foreign admixture. All the region was idolatrous, and the gods which were worshipped there were those worshipped throughout Greece; the miracle led them to suppose the gods had come down, since it was evidently beyond human ability and they had no other way of accounting for it than by supposing that their gods had personally appeared. Many of their gods were heroes whom they worshipped after they were dead, Barnes says, and it was common among them to suppose that the gods appeared to men in human form: the poems of Homer and Virgil are filled with accounts of such appearances, and the only way in which they supposed the gods to take knowledge of human affairs and to aid men was by their personally appearing in this form. He quotes Homer in Cowper's version, that in similitude of strangers oft the gods, who can with ease all shapes assume, repair to populous cities, where they mark the outrageous and the righteous deeds of men; and adds that among the Hindoos the opinion has been prevalent that there have been many incarnations of their gods. Ellicott says the modus operandi of the miracle reminds us of the paralytic, the cripple at Bethesda and the lame man in the third chapter: the command, which would have seemed a mockery to one who did not rise beyond the limits of experience, is obeyed by the will that had been inspired by the new power of faith. The natural inference from the special fact recorded in the next verse, Ellicott says, is that the command was given in Greek, and therefore that Paul had taught in that language; and the two verbs differ in their tense, he leaped, as with a single bound, and then continued walking. On the next verse Ellicott says the fact of the Lycaonian speech is clearly recorded with a definite purpose, and no explanation seems so natural as that which assumes it to be given as accounting for the passive attitude of the Apostles till what was then said had borne its fruit in acts. It will be admitted by all who are not under the influence of a theory, he says, that this serves almost as a crucial instance, showing that the gift of tongues, which Paul possessed so largely, did not consist in a supernatural knowledge of every provincial patois with which he came in contact; it is clear that he might easily have learnt afterwards, from those who knew both languages, the meaning of what at the time was unintelligible. To suppose, as some have done, that the Apostles, understanding what was said, acquiesced in the preparations for sacrifice in order that they might afterwards make their protest as with a greater dramatic effect, is at variance with the natural impression made by the narrative, Ellicott says, and, it need scarcely be said, with any worthy conception of Paul's character. The diglottic character of the people, here and in other Asiatic provinces of the empire, would make it perfectly natural that they should speak to one another in their own dialect, while Greek served for their intercourse with strangers; and the speech of Lycaonia is said to have had affinities with Assyrian. The belief which the words expressed was characteristic of the rude simplicity of the Lycaonians, Ellicott says: no such cry would have been possible in the great cities where the confluence of a debased polytheism and philosophical speculation had ended in utter scepticism. And the form which the belief took was in accordance with the old legends of the district: there, according to the myth which Ovid had recently revived and adorned, Zeus and Hermes had come in human guise and been received by Baucis and Philemon, and left tokens of their favour; and we find from the poem that the place where they had dwelt was looked on as a shrine to which devout worshippers made their pilgrimages and where they left their votive offerings. Robertson says upright is a predicate adjective, and that in this sense the old physicians frequently use the word for erect or straight; Paul spoke in a loud voice so that all could hear and know. He leaped up and walked is rather, he leaped up with a single bound and began to walk, the second aorist middle of a late verb and the inchoative imperfect of the common verb to walk around, and this graphic picture is concealed by the usual English rendering. It is possible that Luke obtained the vivid report of this incident from Timothy, Robertson says, who may have witnessed it and who was probably converted during Paul's stay here; his father was a prominent Greek, and his mother Eunice, possibly a widow, may have lived here with her mother Lois. On the next verse Robertson says they elevated their voices in their excitement, and that the adverb rendered in the speech of Lycaonia is found here alone but formed regularly like the adverbs for in Hebrew, in Greek and in Latin. Paul was speaking in Greek, of course, but the excitement of the crowd over the miracle made them cry out in their native tongue, which Paul and Barnabas did not understand; hence it was not till preparations for offering sacrifice to them had begun that Paul understood the new role in which he and Barnabas were held. In this primitive state the people hold to the old Graeco-Roman mythology, Robertson says, and the story of Baucis and Philemon tells how Zeus and Hermes visited in human form the neighbouring region of Phrygia; Zeus had a temple in Lystra.

Clarke and Wesley take the added clause, the language and the blindness. After the clause said with a loud voice, Clarke says, the following is found in two uncials and several others, either in the text or margin: I say unto thee, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, stand upright on thy feet. This reading is also in several versions, and though it may not stand on such evidence as to entitle it to a place in the text, yet it is not likely that Paul would not have used the sacred name on such an occasion, especially as this appears to have been the usual form. He leaped and walked, Clarke says, giving the fullest proof of his restoration; his leaping, however, might have been through joy of having received his cure. On the next verse Clarke says what the speech of Lycaonia was has puzzled the learned not a little: one scholar thinks it was a corrupt Greek dialect, since Greek was the general language of Asia Minor, while another, who has written a dissertation expressly on the subject, thinks it was the same language as that of the Cappadocians, which was mingled with Syriac. That it was no dialect of the Greek must be evident from the circumstance of its being here distinguished from it, Clarke argues; we have sufficient proofs from ancient authors that most of these provinces used different languages, and every search after the language of Lycaonia must be, at this distance of time, fruitless. From this, and from all heathen antiquity, Clarke says, it is evident that the heathen did not consider the Divine nature, how low soever they rated it, to be like the human nature, and that they imagined these celestial beings often assumed human forms to visit men, in order to punish the evil and reward the good. The Metamorphoses of Ovid are full of such visitations, and so are Homer and Virgil; the angels visiting Abraham, Jacob and Lot might have been the foundation on which most of these heathen fictions were built. Clarke quotes the same lines of Homer in Cowper's version about the gods repairing to populous cities in the similitude of strangers, and a passage of Ovid in Dryden's version in which Jupiter says he will descend in hope to prove the loud complaint a lie and, disguised in human shape, travelled round the world and found more than he had heard; this last, Clarke says, seems to be copied from the account in Genesis of the Lord going down to see whether Sodom had done according to the cry of it. It was a settled belief among the Egyptians that their gods descended to the earth in the likeness of men or of sacred animals, Clarke adds, and the Hindoo incarnations prove how generally this opinion had prevailed, so that we need not wonder to find it in Lycaonia. Wesley says the gods are come down is what the heathens supposed they frequently did, Jupiter especially; but how amazingly does the prince of darkness blind the minds of them that believe not, since the Jews would not own Christ's Godhead though they saw him work numberless miracles, while on the other hand the heathens, seeing mere men work one miracle, were for deifying them immediately.

debates: What the speech of Lycaonia was. Barnes takes it for a mixture of Greek and Syriac, the Greek of the region being corrupted by the nearness of Syria; Clarke argues that it cannot be a dialect of Greek at all, since Luke distinguishes it from Greek, canvasses two scholarly opinions and concludes that the search must at this distance of time be fruitless; Ellicott reports an affinity with Assyrian and explains the use of it by the diglottic habit of the people; Robertson only classes the adverb with those for in Hebrew and in Latin.

Whether the apostles understood the cry. Ellicott makes the recorded fact of the dialect the explanation of their passivity, and calls it almost a crucial instance that the gift of tongues did not include every provincial patois, rejecting as unworthy the view that they understood and waited for a more dramatic moment to protest; Robertson agrees that they did not understand until the sacrifice was being prepared; the others do not raise the question.

Whether the added clause about the name of the Lord Jesus belongs to the text. Clarke says the evidence does not entitle it to a place, while judging it unlikely that Paul omitted the sacred name on such an occasion; Calvin, finding it in many old books of great credit, thinks Luke wrote it and that it has dropped out of the printed copies; Barnes and Ellicott comment on the verse without it.

Where the pagan expectation of visiting gods came from. Clarke derives the whole family of fictions from the angels who visited Abraham, Jacob and Lot; Calvin says the poets turned into fables what the fathers had taught concerning angels, with Satan's help; Ellicott and Robertson look no further than the local myth of Zeus and Hermes entertained by Baucis and Philemon; Barnes explains it from the belief that the gods took knowledge of human affairs only by appearing in person.
outliers: Barnes and Clarke quote the identical four lines of Homer in the identical English version and both then point to the incarnations of the Hindu gods, an agreement too close to be independent.

Wesley alone sets the two errors against each other, that the Jews would not own Christ's Godhead though they saw him work numberless miracles, while the heathen seeing mere men work one were for deifying them immediately.

Robertson alone guesses at Luke's informant, suggesting that the vivid detail came from Timothy, who may have witnessed the healing and was probably converted during this stay, and naming his Greek father and his mother and grandmother.
Calvin alone reads the scene as an argument for the scarcity of miracles, that the Lord would have only a few wrought and those for a short time, lest the lust of men drag them to a contrary end.
themes: the gods are come down in the likeness of men
the gift of tongues and provincial dialects

12.pericope_label: And they called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercurius, because he was the chief speaker. Then the priest of Jupiter, which was before their city, brought oxen and garlands unto the gates, and would have done sacrifice with the people.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the appearance of the two men and the motive of the priest. Gill says they called Barnabas Jupiter, the supreme God, and it may be because Barnabas was the oldest man, of the tallest stature and largest bulk, and made the best figure, whereas Paul was younger, of a low stature and mean appearance. On the next verse Gill says it was not the priest that was before the city but Jupiter, and the phrase denotes either his presidency over the city, so that the Arabic version renders it, who was the chief god of their city, or the place where his image stood, which was out of the city and so may be said to be before it, the Syriac version rendering it, who was without the city. Calvin says that though Luke doth not express with what affection this priest was moved to be so diligent, yet it is to be thought that, forasmuch as there was great hope of most plentiful gain offered, he was moved with covetousness; for he had great hope of gain in time to come if it should be noised abroad that Jupiter appeared there, since this opinion would by and by have followed, that Jupiter was more delighted in the temple of Lystra than in any other. So soon as such superstition hath once filled the minds of men, Calvin says, they spare no cost to offer sacrifice: the world is indeed of itself inclined to this, but then came the sacrificing priests, who are like fans and bellows. And it is not to be doubted but that the whole multitude was moved with ambition, to be so desirous to offer sacrifice to Paul under the name of Jupiter, that their city might be the more famous and noble; hence hath Satan so great liberty to deceive, whilst that the sacrificing priests set nets to get gain, and the people are delighted to have errors confirmed.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the two gods, the temple and the sacrifice. Barnes says Jupiter was represented as the most powerful of all the gods of the ancients, the son of Saturn and Ops, educated in a cave on Mount Ida in Crete, and that his worship was almost universal: he was the Ammon of Africa, the Belus of Babylon, the Osiris of Egypt, his common appellation was the father of gods and men, and he was usually represented sitting upon a golden or an ivory throne, holding in one hand a thunderbolt and in the other a sceptre of cypress, his power extending over the other gods, everything being subservient to his will except the fates. There is abundant proof that he was worshipped in the region of Lycaonia and throughout Asia Minor, Barnes says, and there was besides a fable among the inhabitants of Lycaonia that Jupiter and Mercury had once visited that place and been received by Philemon, the whole fable being related by Ovid. Mercury, called by the Greeks Hermes, was a celebrated god of antiquity, the son of Jupiter and Maia; he was the messenger of the gods and of Jupiter in particular, the patron of travellers and shepherds, he conducted the souls of the dead into the infernal regions, he presided over orators and declaimers and merchants, and he was also the god of thieves, pickpockets and all dishonest persons; he was regarded as the god of eloquence, and as light, rapid and quick in his movements. The conjecture of Chrysostom is, Barnes says, that Barnabas was a large, athletic man and was hence taken for Jupiter, and Paul was small in his person and was hence supposed to be Mercury; the office of Mercury was to deliver the messages of the gods, and as Paul only had been discoursing he was supposed to be Mercury. On the next verse Barnes says the priest of Jupiter was he whose office it was to conduct the worship of Jupiter by offering sacrifices, and that the word which refers not to the priest but to Jupiter: the temple or image of Jupiter was in front of their city, or near the gates, since ancient cities were supposed to be under the protection of particular gods and their image or a temple for their worship was placed commonly in a conspicuous place at the entrance of the city. He brought oxen, probably two, one to be sacrificed to each, it being common to sacrifice bullocks to Jupiter; the victims of sacrifice were usually decorated with ribands and chaplets of flowers; unto the gates means the gates of the city, where were the images or temple of the gods. And here we have a remarkable and most affecting instance of the folly and stupidity of idolatry, Barnes says. Ellicott notes that Luke gives, as was natural, the Greek forms, Zeus and Hermes, and that the main reason for the assignment of the two names was that the listeners recognised in Paul the gift of eloquence, which was the special attribute of Hermes. Possibly also, unlike as were the weak bodily presence and the many infirmities of the Apostle to the sculptured grace with which we are familiar as belonging to the sandalled messenger of the gods, young and beautiful and agile, there may have been something in the taller stature and more stately presence of Barnabas which impressed them with the sense of a dignity like that of Jupiter. In any case, Ellicott says, we must remember that the masterpieces of Greek art were not likely to have found their way to a Lycaonian village, and that the Hermes of Lystra may have borne the same relation to that of Athens and Corinth as the grotesque Madonna of some Italian wayside shrine does to the masterpieces of Raphael: real idolatry cares little about the aesthetic beauty of the objects of its worship, and the Lycaonians were genuine idolaters. The chief speaker is literally the ruler of speech, taking the chief part in it. On the next verse Ellicott says the latter clause probably describes the position of the Temple of Zeus, standing at the entrance of the city as the shrine of its protecting deity, and that the identical phrase used by Luke is found in Greek inscriptions at Ephesus. The garlands were the well-known fillets, so familiar to us in ancient sculptures, commonly made of white wool, sometimes interwoven with leaves and flowers, and the priests, attendants, doors and altars were often decorated in the same way; the gates, the form of the Greek implying that they were the folding-doors of a large entrance, were probably those which led into the court-yard of the house where the Apostles were dwelling, and the whole action is well represented in Raphael's well-known cartoon.
