Oxen were, in Greek ritual, the right victims for both Zeus and Hermes, Ellicott says, and the sacrifice would have involved cutting the throats of the oxen, catching the blood in a deep dish and pouring it upon an altar; there may have been such an altar in the court-yard, or one may have been improvised for the occasion. Robertson says they began to call Barnabas Jupiter because he was the older and the more imposing in appearance, Paul admitting that he was not impressive in looks; Mercury was the messenger of the gods and the spokesman of Zeus, of beautiful appearance and eloquent in speech, the inventor of speech in legend, and our word hermeneutics comes from this word. Paul was clearly the leader of the talk, Robertson says, so it seemed a clear case to the natives — if preachers always knew what people really think of them; and whether Paul was alluding to his experience in Lystra or not in the Galatian letter, certainly they did receive him as an angel of God, as if Mercury in reality. On the next verse Robertson says the god is identified with his temple, that he had a statue and temple there, that the garlands were probably to put on the oxen before they were slain, and that the imperfect means the priest wanted to offer sacrifice and was planning to do it, his purpose now becoming plain to Paul and Barnabas.

Clarke and Wesley take the two deities, the guardian title and the garlands. The heathens supposed that Jupiter and Mercury were the gods who most frequently assumed the human form, Clarke says, and Jupiter was accustomed to take Mercury with him on such expeditions; Jupiter was the supreme god of the heathens and Mercury was by them considered the god of eloquence, and the ancient fable represents Jupiter and Mercury coming to this very region, where they were entertained by Lycaon, from whom the Lycaonians derived their name. As the ancients usually represented Jupiter as rather an aged man, large, noble and majestic, and Mercury young, light and active, the conjecture of Chrysostom is very probable, Clarke says, that Barnabas was a large, noble, well-made man, and probably in years, and Paul young, active and eloquent, on which account they termed the former Jupiter and the latter Mercury. That Mercury was eloquent and powerful in his words is allowed by the heathens, Clarke adds, and the very epithet that is applied here to Paul, that he was the chief or leader of the discourse, was applied to Mercury: he cites one author for the saying that the god who is leader of words is Hermes, and another for the saying that we know Mercury is powerful both in his voice and eloquence. With the Lycaonians the actions of these apostles proved them to be gods, and the different parts they took appeared to fix their character, so that one was judged to be Jupiter and the other Mercury. On the next verse Clarke says there is a meaning here which ordinary readers will not readily apprehend: many cities were put under the protection of a particular deity, and the image of that deity placed at the entrance to signify that he was the guardian and protector, and to this Luke, everywhere as accurate as he is circumstantial, refers. Lystra, it appears, was under the guardianship of Jupiter of the Gate, which Luke translates as the Jupiter that was before the city, another term for Jupiter the guardian; all these deities, according to the attributes they sustained, had their peculiar priests, rites and sacrifices, so that Jupiter the thunderer had a different service from Jove the guardian. Hence we can see with what accuracy Luke wrote, Clarke says: the person who was going to offer them sacrifice was the priest of Jupiter the guardian, under whose guardianship the city of Lystra was, and whom the priest supposed had visited the city in a human form. A beautiful figure of such an image of Jupiter as, Clarke supposes, stood before the gate of Lystra still remains, and an engraving of it may be seen in a collection of inscriptions: Jupiter is represented naked, sitting on a curule chair, in his right hand he holds his thunder and a long staff in his left, at his right stands the eagle prepared for flight, and above are the winged cap and caduceus of Mercury, the base bearing the inscription, Jupiter, the guardian of the house of Augustus. Oxen and garlands means oxen adorned with flowers, their horns gilded and neck bound about with fillets, as was the custom in sacrificial rites, Clarke says, and they also crowned the gods themselves, the priests, and gates of the temples, with flowers; of this method of adorning the victims there are numerous examples in the Greek and Latin writers, and he quotes three passages of Ovid and one of Virgil in English verse on the fairest victim brought to the altar with a purple filet, flowery garlands and gilded horns. At the time of worship the Hindoo priests place garlands of flowers on the head of the image, Clarke adds; whether the garlands here were intended to decorate the oxen or the apostles we cannot say, but in either case the conduct of the Lycaonians was conformable to that of the modern Hindoos. Wesley says the priest of Jupiter, whose temple and image were just without the gate of the city, brought garlands to put on the victims, and bulls, the usual offerings to Jupiter.

debates: Which gates the oxen were brought to. Barnes takes them for the gates of the city, where the images or temple of the gods stood; Ellicott argues from the form of the Greek that they were the folding-doors of a large entrance, probably those leading into the court-yard of the house where the Apostles were lodging; Robertson and Wesley leave the question and speak only of the sacrifice.

What the garlands were for. Robertson says they were probably to put on the oxen before they were slain, and Wesley the same; Ellicott identifies them with the white woollen fillets of the sculptures and notes that priests, attendants, doors and altars were dressed the same way; Barnes says the victims were usually decorated with ribands and chaplets of flowers; Clarke refuses to decide whether they were meant for the oxen or for the apostles.

Why the names were assigned as they were. All agree that Paul was Mercury because he did the speaking; on the physical contrast, Gill has Barnabas oldest, tallest and bulkiest against a Paul of low stature and mean appearance, Robertson has him older and more imposing, and Barnes and Clarke both credit the conjecture to an early Greek father, while Ellicott adds that the local images were probably too crude for any close comparison to have been in view.

What the phrase before their city means. Clarke takes it as Luke's rendering of a technical cult title of Jupiter the guardian, whose image stood at the entrance, and makes it evidence of Luke's accuracy; Ellicott independently reports the identical phrase from Greek inscriptions at Ephesus; Barnes and Gill establish only that the words describe Jupiter and not the priest, Gill citing two versions that read it differently; Robertson identifies the god with his temple.
outliers: Clarke alone finds that the phrase Luke uses of Paul, the leader of the discourse, was a standing title of Hermes, and produces two ancient authors who use it of him.

Ellicott alone raises the question of what the local idols actually looked like, warning that the masterpieces of Greek art were unlikely to have reached a Lycaonian village and that real idolatry cares little about the beauty of what it worships.

Calvin alone asks what the priest stood to gain, judging him moved by covetousness, since a report that Jupiter had appeared at Lystra would make its temple the more frequented; and he charges the crowd with ambition for their city's fame, calling the sacrificing priests fans and bellows to a fire the world lights of itself.

Barnes alone completes Mercury's portfolio past the point of dignity, adding to the messenger of the gods and the patron of orators and merchants the god of thieves, pickpockets and all dishonest persons.
themes: because he was the chief speaker
the priest of Jupiter before the city
oxen and garlands unto the gates

14.pericope_label: Which when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of, they rent their clothes, and ran in among the people, crying out, and saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the title of apostle and the meaning of vanity. Gill says the apostles heard of it quickly, such a multitude being about the doors of the house where they were, and it may be observed that Barnabas is here called an apostle and is placed before Paul, not as being greater than he, but because of the opinion these heathens had of him; they rent their clothes as the Jews did, and were obliged to do, when they heard any blasphemy. On the next verse Gill says they asked why do ye these things, that is, bring these oxen and garlands and attempt to offer sacrifice, and that they said this not as arguing with them calmly and mildly, but with a mixture of indignation, heat and zeal, as displeased with and detesting and abhorring what they were about to do. Calvin says that in renting their garments and leaping into the midst of the multitude it appeareth how zealous they were for the glory of God, since, not content only to speak to the people, they troubled the preparation of the sacrifice so much as they were able. It cometh to pass sometimes that even hypocrites refuse excessive honour, Calvin says, but they rather provoke the simple to give it them with their feigned modesty; there was no such thing in Paul and Barnabas, for they declared, both by words and by all gesture of body, that they were so far from taking pleasure in that worship that they did utterly detest it. This is holy anger, wherewith the servants of God must be inflamed so often as they see his glory profaned and overthrown by the sacrileges of men, Calvin says, and no man shall be able otherwise to serve God sincerely and faithfully unless he put on that affection of jealousy whereof Paul speaketh, that those men to whom the Lord hath committed the charge of his Church be no less courageous and stout to defend the glory of their Lord than a husband is vigilant to defend his wife's chastity. Though the teachers of the Church ought especially to be imbued with zeal, he adds, yet there is no one of the godly which ought not to be sore displeased when he seeth the worship of God polluted or given to some other. When the world abuseth the names and persons of holy men unto superstition it thinketh it doth them a great pleasure, Calvin says, but it is greatly deceived, for they will stand up first against their worshippers; and there can be no greater injury done to them than when the honour which is taken from God is given to them. It appeareth by other places of Scripture that renting the garments was a custom among the men of the east country, so often as they would by external gesture express either great sorrow or detesting of any thing. When Luke calleth Barnabas an apostle together with Paul, Calvin says, he extendeth the signification of the word farther than unto the chief order which Christ appointed in his Church, like as Paul maketh Andronicus and Junias excellent among the apostles; but if we should speak properly, they were evangelists and not apostles, unless peradventure, because Barnabas was made Paul's fellow in office, we place them both in like degree. On the next verse Calvin says they begin with a reprehension, as the matter did require, then show to what end they were sent, then preach concerning the only God, and lastly teach that this ignorance was without excuse. The reason they allege seemeth cold, Calvin admits, for it were an easy matter to gather thence that it is not unlawful to worship those who are delivered from human miseries by death, and by this means all the superstitions of the Gentiles should stand untouched, which were wont to count none gods but those who were dead; with the same colour also have the Papists coloured their idolatry, who worship rather the dead men's bones, stones and wood, than living men in whose nostrils is breath. I answer, Calvin says, that Paul and Barnabas drew this argument from the matter which was now in hand: we be miserable men, therefore you do falsely and filthily imagine us to be gods. If idolatry be handled generally, this shall be a perpetual reason to condemn it, that the perfect and whole worship of godliness is due to God alone. They call all that vain which men have invented to themselves of their own brain, Calvin says, and we must mark this definition, that all religion is vain which departeth and degenerateth from the pure and simple Word of God; because God is no otherwise rightly worshipped than according to his appointment, it followeth that so soon as men depart from that worship which God hath commanded, they are wearied foolishly and vainly with a vain and unprofitable labour. This was the cause that sincere and perfect godliness was never found in the more part of the world, Calvin says: they stood only about the removing of the old idolatry, and the other thing was neglected, to bring men unto the true God alone after they had forsaken idols. They turned the name of an idol sometimes into the name of God, but under that colour they did nevertheless cherish the old errors: the priests of France begat the single life of great Cybele, nuns came in place of the vestal virgins, the church of All Saints succeeded the Pantheon, and at length came in the multitude of gods, who they thought would be lawful and tolerable if they had once decked them with the titles of saints. Corruptions are not by this means purged, Calvin says, neither are the stables, both profane and full of filth, turned into the temple of God, but the name of God is mixed with profane pollutions.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the rending, the word for like passions, and the argument of the speech. Barnes says Barnabas is called an apostle because he was sent forth by the church on a particular message, not because he had been chosen to the peculiar work of the apostleship, to bear witness to the life and resurrection of Christ; they rent their clothes as an expression of their abhorrence of what the people were doing, and of their deep grief that they should thus debase themselves by offering worship to men. On the next verse Barnes says the question is an expression of solemn remonstrance at the folly of their conduct in worshipping those who were men, and that the abhorrence which they evinced at this may throw strong light on the rank and character of the Lord Jesus Christ: when an offer was made to worship Paul and Barnabas they shrank from it with strong expressions of indignation and abhorrence, yet when similar worship was offered to the Lord Jesus, when he was addressed by Thomas in the language of worship, My Lord and my God, he commended the disciple and uttered not the slightest reproof, nay, he approved it and expressed his approbation of others who should also do it. How can this difference be accounted for, Barnes asks, except on the supposition that the Lord Jesus was Divine? Would he, if a mere man, receive homage as God, when his disciples rejected it with horror? Of like passions with you means we are men like yourselves, Barnes says: the word passions here means simply that they had the common feelings and propensities of men, and it does not mean that they were subject to any improper passions, to ill temper and the like, as some have supposed, but that they did not pretend to be gods; the Latin Vulgate renders it, we are mortal like yourselves, and the expression stands opposed to the proper conception of God, who is not subject to these affections. Idols are often called vanities or vain things, and often a lie, as opposed to the living and true God, because they are unreal, because they have no power to help, because confidence in them is vain. This doctrine, that there was one God who had made all things, was new to them, Barnes says: they worshipped multitudes of divinities, and though they regarded Jupiter as the father of gods and men, yet they had no conception that all things had been formed from nothing by the will of one Infinite Being. Ellicott says the apostles were, we may believe, in the house, within the court-yard, and therefore did not see the sacrificial procession, but they heard the noise of the multitude, perhaps also of some sacrificial hymn, and asked what it meant. The act of renting the clothes is obviously recorded as that of men who are startled and surprised, Ellicott says, and is altogether incompatible with the theory that they knew that they had been taken for deities and were expecting such honours; it was the extremest expression of horror, hardly ever used except in deprecation of spoken or acted blasphemy, and how far it would be fully understood by the heathen population of Lystra may be a question, but its very strangeness would startle and arrest them. On the next verse Ellicott says it is natural to suppose that the words were spoken in the Greek in which Luke records them, and therefore that Paul's previous teaching had been in the same language, the metrical structure of the close of the speech leaving hardly a shadow of doubt on this point. The word rendered of like passions expresses participation in all the passive conditions of human life as well as in what are commonly known as passions, and there is a striking parallelism between Paul's language here and that of Peter to Cornelius. The demonstrative pronoun in these vanities implies a corresponding gesture, Ellicott says, the Apostle pointing to all the pomp and pageantry of the intended sacrifice; the words vanity and vain were almost the invariable terms used by Jews to describe the emptiness and worthlessness of heathen worship. In contrast with these dead and dumb things the Apostle calls on them to turn to God, who truly lives and acts and is the source of all life and power, the Maker of heaven and earth, the Giver of all good gifts, the Judge of all evil deeds; and in contrast alike with the popular polytheism which assigned heaven, and earth, and sea to different deities, and with the speculative Pantheism which excluded will and purpose from its conception of the Godhead, he proclaims the One God as having every attribute of personal Life and Being. Robertson says such elaborate preparation spread rumours and some who spoke Greek told Paul and Barnabas, and that it is possible the priest of Jupiter may have sent a formal request that the visiting gods might come out to the statue by the temple gates to make it a grand occasion. They rent their garments like the high priest, as if an act of sacrilege was about to be committed — it was strange conduct for the supposed gods, Robertson says; and sprang forth is an ingressive aorist of an old verb found here only in the New Testament, all a sign of grief and horror with loud outcries. On the next verse he says Sirs is literally Men, abrupt but courteous, and that of like passions means of like nature more exactly, and affected by like sensations, not gods at all; their conduct was more serious than the obeisance of Cornelius to Peter. There is no and in the Greek before the participle, Robertson notes, only gospelizing you: they are not gods but evangelists. Here we have Paul's message to a pagan audience without the Jewish environment, he says, and he makes the same line of argument seen at Athens and in Romans. He boldly calls the worship of Jupiter and Mercury and all idols vain or empty things, pointing to the statues and the temple; they must go the whole way, since our God is a live God, not a dead statue, and the one God is alive and is the Creator of the Universe, just as Paul will argue in Athens.

Clarke and Wesley take the disputed phrase and the vanities. This saying of the apostles has been most strangely perverted, Clarke says: a pious commentator, taking the word passion in its vulgar and most improper sense of a bad temper or an evil propensity, and supposing that these holy men wished to confess that they also had many sinful infirmities and wrong tempers, endeavours to illustrate this sense of the word by appealing to the contention of Paul and Barnabas. But the expression means no more than, we are truly human beings, with the same powers and appetites as your own, need food and raiment as you do, and are all mortal like yourselves. That ye should turn from these vanities means from these idols and false gods, Clarke says, and how often false gods and idolatry are termed vanity in the Scriptures no careful reader of the Bible needs to be told. What a bold saying was this in the presence of a heathen mob intent on performing an act of their superstitious worship, in which they no doubt thought the safety of the state was concerned. Clarke retells the ancient fable of Jupiter visiting Lycaonia in human shape, being received and doubted by Lycaon, who slew an ambassador and served his flesh at table, and was turned into a wolf for the insult, from which fable the province took its name; the simple people, seeing such proofs of supernatural power in the miracles wrought by Barnabas and Paul, thought that Jupiter had again visited them, and feared lest they should meet with his indignation should they neglect duly to honour him. As the people took them for gods, Clarke says, it was necessary for the apostles to show that they were but men, and this is the whole that is meant by the phrase men of like passions, fellow mortals, which has been so pitifully mistaken by some and abused by others. The living God is widely different from those stocks and stones which were objects of their worship, he adds, and as all things were made by his power, so all subsist by his providence, and to him alone all worship, honour and glory are due. Wesley says to turn from these vanities means from worshipping any but the true God, and that Paul does not deign to call them gods; unto the living God, not like these dead idols, who made the heaven and the earth, the sea, each of which they supposed to have its own gods.

Chrysostom takes the vehemence of the apostles and the shape of the speech. Mark the vehemence with which all this is done by the Apostles, he says: they rent their clothes, ran in, cried out, all from strong affection of the soul, revolted by the things that were done. For it was a grief, indeed a grief inconsolable, that they should needs be thought gods and introduce idolatry, the very thing which they came to destroy; this also was a contrivance of the devil, but he did not prevail. But what say they? We also are men of like passions with you: at the very outset they overthrew the evil, Chrysostom says, for they said not simply Men, but As ye. Then, that they may not seem to honour the gods, hear what they add, preaching unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, who made heaven, the sea, and all things that are therein. Observe how they nowhere mention things invisible, Chrysostom says, for they had learnt that one should study not so much to say somewhat worthy of God as to say what is profitable for the hearers. What then, if he be Maker of all things, why does he not also attend to these things by his Providence? He answers, who in times past suffered all nations to walk in their own ways; but wherefore he suffered them, this he does not say, for at present he keeps to the matter of immediate importance, nowhere bringing in the name of Christ. Observe, Chrysostom says, he does not wish to swell the accusation against them, but rather that they themselves should refer all to God; and see how covertly he puts the accusation in the words, in that he did good, for if God did this he could not have let them alone, and on the contrary they ought to be punished, since, enjoying so great benefits, they had not acknowledged him, not even as their feeder. With large liberality the food is given, he adds, not merely for a frugal sufficiency nor stinted by the need. Chrysostom carries the comment on through the stoning: the Jews from Antioch and Iconium are children of the devil, that not in their own cities only but also beyond them they did these things, and as much made it their study to make an end of the preaching as the Apostles were in earnest to establish it. In the very city in which they received this reverence, in the same were they thus terribly ill treated, he says, and this also profited the beholders; and when Paul rose up and came into the city, here is fulfilled the saying, My grace is sufficient for thee, for my strength is made perfect in weakness — greater this than the raising of the lame man.

debates: What the torn clothes prove. Chrysostom takes them for the overflow of a soul revolted at being thought a god; Ellicott makes the act evidence that the two were startled and surprised, and altogether incompatible with the theory that they had understood the cry and were waiting for a dramatic moment; Robertson says drily that it was strange conduct for the supposed gods; Calvin contrasts it with the feigned modesty of hypocrites who refuse honour in a way that makes the simple press it harder.

In what sense Barnabas is an apostle. Gill notes only that he is named before Paul because of the opinion the heathen had of him; Barnes says he is called an apostle because sent forth by the church on a particular message, not as a witness of the resurrection; Calvin says the word is extended beyond the order Christ appointed and that properly the two were evangelists, allowing that Barnabas may be called an apostle as Paul's fellow in office.

What of like passions means. Clarke attacks a commentator who took passion in its vulgar sense of bad temper and read the words as a confession of sinful infirmity, citing the later quarrel of Paul and Barnabas for proof; Barnes rejects the same reading and cites the Latin, we are mortal like yourselves; Robertson makes it of like nature, affected by like sensations; Ellicott takes it of all the passive conditions of human life and notes the parallel with Peter's words to Cornelius.

How the apostles learned what was happening. Ellicott has them indoors in the courtyard, hearing the noise and perhaps a sacrificial hymn and asking what it meant; Robertson supposes Greek-speaking bystanders told them, and adds that the priest may have sent a formal invitation for the visiting gods to come out to the statue and make a grand occasion of it.
outliers: Barnes alone turns the apostles' horror into an argument for the deity of Christ, setting their refusal of worship beside the commendation Thomas received for saying My Lord and my God, and asking how the difference can be accounted for on any other supposition.

Calvin alone carries the rebuke forward to the veneration of saints, arguing that the honour taken from God and given to holy men is the greatest injury that can be done them, and that they will stand up first against their own worshippers.

Chrysostom alone reads the speech by what is missing from it, that nothing is said of things invisible and the name of Christ is nowhere brought in, because the apostles had learnt to study not what is worthy of God but what is profitable for the hearers.

Ellicott alone infers the language of the whole mission from the metrical shape of the speech's close, arguing that the words were spoken in the Greek Luke records and therefore that Paul had been teaching in Greek all along.
themes: men of like passions with you
the living God which made heaven and earth

16.pericope_label: Who in times past suffered all nations to walk in their own ways. Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the long permission and the reach of natural testimony. Gill says in times past means for many hundred years past, ever since God chose and separated the people of Israel from the rest of the nations to be a peculiar people to himself. On the next verse Gill says he left not himself without witness of his kindness and goodness to them during this long interval: they had not the written law, yet they were not destitute of the law of nature, and had besides many instances of providential goodness by which they might have known God, and should have been thankful to him and glorified him as God, and not have worshipped the idols of their own hands; the goodness of God should have led them to repentance, and not have been abused to so many wicked purposes as it had been. Calvin says that because the men of Lystra might object that this God was unknown hitherto, Paul and Barnabas prevent them and say that all men wandered indeed in darkness and that all mankind was stricken with blindness, but deny that any judgment must be founded on the perverse ignorance of the world. These were two no small lets for the unbelievers, Calvin says, long antiquity of time and the consent almost of all nations, and Paul and Barnabas remove both: if men have erred many ages, and if the world have wandered without reason and judgment, let not therefore the truth of God, when it appeareth, be less precious to you, for seeing that it is eternal and is not changed, it is an unmeet thing that the long prescription of years should be set against it. There is no cause why the conspiracy of all the whole world should keep you from coming to the right way, he says: blindness hath got the upper hand among all people, but God doth now give light to you. When he calleth errors the ways of men, Calvin says, we are plainly taught what the wisdom and understanding of man's mind can do in beholding and keeping the way of salvation: all nations have walked in their own ways, that is, they have wandered in darkness and death, and it is all one as if he should say that there is no sparkle of true reason in all the whole world. Therefore there is but one rule of true godliness, that the faithful, casting from them all confidence in their own wit, do submit themselves to God; for the ways of men are now as they were in times past, and the examples of all times teach how miserably blind those men be who have not the word of God to give them light, though they think they can pass other men in quickness of sight. But Paul and Barnabas show no cause here why the Lord suffered the world to err so long, Calvin says, and assuredly we must count the will of God alone the chiefest law of equity: God hath always a good reason for his works, but because it is oftentimes hid from us, it is our duty reverently to wonder at his secret counsel. We must confess that the world deserved such destruction, but there can no other reason be brought why the Lord had mercy rather on one age than on another, save only because it seemed good to him that it should be so; therefore Paul calleth that time which was appointed of God for preaching the gospel the time of fullness, lest any other opportunity be sought. So the cavil of the Papists is refuted, Calvin adds, who say that it cannot be that God suffered his Church to err so long; for whence came the Gentiles but from the ark of Noah, when there was a singular purity of the Church? On the next verse Calvin says Paul and Barnabas take from the Gentiles the pretext of ignorance, for however greatly men please themselves in their own inventions, being at length convicted of error they fly unto this fortress, that no blame ought to be imputed to them but that God was rather cruel, who did not vouchsafe so much as with one hiss to call back those he saw perishing. Paul and Barnabas anticipate this frivolous objection when they show that God lay hid in such sort that he still bare witness of himself and his divinity. We must see how these two things can hang together, Calvin says, for if God bare witness of himself he did not suffer, so much as in him lay, the world to err. I answer that this kind of testimony was such as made men without excuse, and yet was not sufficient to salvation; for faith is not conceived by the bare beholding of the heaven and earth, but by the hearing of the word, whereupon it followeth that men are brought by the direction of the word alone unto that knowledge of Almighty God which bringeth salvation. And yet this letteth not but that they may be made without excuse even without the word, who, though they be naturally deprived of light, are blind notwithstanding through their own malice. Because the light of doctrine had been buried long, Calvin says, they say only that God was showed by natural evidences; and it is to be thought that they set forth the magnificence of the works of God as became them, but it was sufficient for Luke to touch the chief points. Neither do I understand it that they treated subtly, after the manner of the philosophers, of the secrets of nature, for they spake unto an unlearned multitude. They take this principle, that in the order of nature there is a certain and evident manifestation of God: in that the earth is watered with rain, in that the heat of the sun causes it to vegetate, in that there cometh such abundance of fruit out of the same yearly, it is thereby gathered for a surety that there is some God who governeth all things, for even the heaven and earth are not moved or governed by their own motion, and much less by fortune. Therefore it remaineth that this wonderful workmanship of nature doth manifestly show the providence of God, Calvin says, and those who said that the world was eternal spake not as they thought, but went about by malicious ingratitude to suppress the glory of God. The ungodliness of men is the more convicted in that God doth not only set before their eyes testimonies of his glory in his works, but doth also appoint all things for their use: why doth the sun shine, why doth the rain fall, why doth the earth bring forth her increase, save only that they may minister to men? Therefore God hath not set man upon earth that he may be an idle beholder of his work, as being set upon a theatre, but to exercise himself in praising the liberality of God whilst he enjoyeth the riches of heaven and earth. To fill the hearts with meat doth signify nothing else but to give food which may satisfy the desires of men, Calvin says, and by this word they mean that God doth give more to men, according to his infinite goodness, than their necessity doth require, meat being given not only to refresh their strength but also to make their hearts merry; and if any object that men do oftentimes rather mourn being hungry than rejoice being full, I answer that that cometh to pass contrary to the order of nature.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the permission, the philosophy of history and the witness of the rain. Barnes says in times past means previous to the gospel, and that suffered all nations means permitted all the Gentiles to conduct themselves without the restraints and instructions of a written law: they were permitted to follow their own reason and passions and their own system of religion, God giving them no written laws and sending them no messengers. Why he did this we cannot determine, Barnes says, but it might have been, among other reasons, to show to the world conclusively the insufficiency of reason to guide men in the matters of religion: the experiment was made under the most favourable circumstances, the most enlightened nations, the Greeks and Romans, being left to pursue the inquiry, and they failed no less than the most degraded tribes of men; the trial was made for four thousand years and attended with the same results everywhere. It showed the need of revelation to guide man, he adds, and it evinced beyond the possibility of mistake the depravity of man, since in all nations and in all circumstances men had shown the same alienation from God; by suffering them to walk in their own ways it was seen that those ways were sin, and that some power more than human was necessary to bring men back to God. On the next verse Barnes says he gave demonstration of his existence and of his moral character by doing good, and that idols did not do good or confer favours and were therefore unworthy of confidence. Rain is one of the evidences of his goodness, Barnes says: man could not cause it, and without it, regulated at proper intervals and in proper quantities, the earth would soon be one wide scene of desolation; there is scarcely anything that more certainly indicates unceasing care and wisdom than the needful and refreshing showers of rain. The sun and stars move by fixed laws whose operation we can see and anticipate, he says, but the falling of rain and dew is regulated by laws which we cannot trace, and seems therefore to be poured, as it were, directly from God's hollow hand; and he quotes a hymn on the showers of blessing sent down to cheer the plains below. Fruitful seasons means seasons when the earth produces abundance, Barnes says, and it is a shining proof of the divine goodness that so few seasons are unfruitful; his ancient covenant God does not forget, though man forgets it and disregards his great Benefactor. The word hearts is here used as a Hebraism to denote persons themselves, and gladness is the comfort arising from the supply of our constantly returning wants: it would be easy for God to withdraw these blessings and leave us to want, and a single deviation from the fullness of benevolence would blast all these comforts. Ellicott says the term rendered all nations is better all the heathen, being that always employed of the nations outside the covenant of Israel, and that we have here the first germ of what may be fairly described as Paul's philosophy of history: the times of ignorance had been permitted by God, and those who had lived in them would be equitably dealt with and judged according to their knowledge. The same thought meets us again in the speech at Athens, Ellicott says, and in Romans in an expanded form as a more complete vindication of the righteousness of God: the ignorance and the sins of the Gentile world had been allowed to run their course, as the Law had been allowed to do its partial and imperfect work among the Jews, as parts of a great divine drama, leading both to feel the need of redemption and preparing both for its reception. On the next verse Ellicott says we have again the outline of what is afterwards expanded in Romans, and that in speaking to peasants like those at Lystra Paul naturally dwells most on the witness given through the divine goodness as manifested in nature, while in addressing philosophers at Athens and at Rome he points to the yet fuller witness of consciousness and conscience. The manuscripts vary, some giving us and our and some you and your, the former being more characteristic of the sympathy which led Paul to identify himself with Gentile as well as Jew, since the joy of harvest was the common inheritance of each. The latter words in the Greek, from giving us rain from heaven, are so distinctly rhythmical that they suggest the thought that Paul quotes from some hymn of praise which he had heard in a harvest or vintage festival, Ellicott says, and which, as with the altar to the Unknown God at Athens, he claims as due to Him whom men ignorantly worshipped. Robertson notes that in the generations gone by uses a perfect middle participle of an old verb found here alone in the New Testament, and that Paul here touches God in history as he did just before in creation: God's hand is on the history of all the nations, Gentile and Jew, only with the Gentiles he withdrew the restraints of his grace in large measure, judgment enough for their sins. This philosophy of history does not mean that God was ignorant or unconcerned, Robertson says; he was biding his time in patience. On the next verse he notes an old compound particle used twice only in the New Testament, and an old adjective for without witness found only here. This witness to God, his doing good, giving rains and fruitful seasons, filling their hearts with food and gladness, they could receive without the help of the Old Testament revelation. Zeus was regarded as the god of rain, Robertson says, and Paul claims the rain and the fruitful seasons as coming from God; Lycaonia was often dry and it would be an appropriate item, and Mercury, as the god of merchandise, was also the dispenser of food. Paul does not talk about laws of nature as if they governed themselves, but he sees the living God behind the drama of the physical world, Robertson says; these simple country people could grasp his ideas as he claims everything for the one true God. Gladness is an old word for good cheer, found in the New Testament only twice, and cheerfulness should be our normal attitude when we consider God's goodness; Paul does not here mention Christ because he had the single definite purpose to dissuade them from worshipping Barnabas and himself.

Clarke and Wesley take the Gentiles, the economy of providence and the objection from antiquity. Clarke says the words we translate all nations should be rendered all the Gentiles, merely to distinguish them from the Jewish people, who, having a revelation, were not left to walk in their own ways, whereas the heathens, who had not a revelation, were suffered to form their creed and mode of worship according to their own caprice. On the next verse Clarke says that though God gave the Gentiles no revelation of his will, yet he continued to govern them by his gracious providence, doing them good in general, giving them rain to fertilise their grounds and fruitful seasons as the result, so that grass grew for the cattle and corn for the service of man. Filling our hearts with food means giving as much food as could reasonably be wished, so that gladness or general happiness was the result, Clarke says: such was the gracious provision made for man at all times that the economy and bounty of the Divine Being were equally evidenced by it. He never gives less than is necessary, nor more than is sufficient; his economy forbids men to waste, by giving them in general no profusion, and his bounty forbids them to want, by giving as much as is sufficient for all the natural wants of his creatures; by not giving too much he prevents luxury and riot, by giving enough he prevents discontent and misery. Thus he does mankind good by causing his rain to descend upon the just and the unjust, Clarke says, and thus he is said not to have left himself without witness, for his providential dealings are the witnesses of his being, his wisdom and his bounty, so that those who continued to worship stocks and stones were without excuse. These were great and striking truths, and into what detail the apostles now went we cannot say, but it is likely that they spoke much more than is here related. Wesley says that in the words who in times past Paul prevents their objection, But if these things are so, we should have heard them from our fathers; that suffered is an awful judgment; that the multitude of them that err does not turn error into truth; and that to walk in their own ways means the idolatries which they had chosen. On the next verse Wesley says the heathens had always from God himself a testimony both of his existence and of his providence: even by punishments he testifies of himself, but more peculiarly by benefits, giving rain, by which air, earth and sea are as it were all joined together, from heaven, the seat of God, to which Paul probably pointed while he spoke, filling the body with food, the soul with gladness.

debates: Whether the reason for the long permission may be asked. Barnes says we cannot determine it and then offers three reasons, to show the insufficiency of reason in religion after a four-thousand-year experiment, to show the need of revelation, and to evince the depravity of man; Calvin says they show no cause here and that we must count the will of God alone the chiefest law of equity, our duty being to wonder reverently at his secret counsel; Ellicott and Robertson describe the permission as a stage in a divine plan without asking why it was so long.

How far the witness of nature reaches. Calvin allows that it made men without excuse but denies that it was sufficient to salvation, since faith comes not by beholding heaven and earth but by hearing the word; Clarke says the providential dealings are witnesses of God's being and bounty, so that those who went on worshipping stocks and stones were without excuse; Ellicott says those who lived in the times of ignorance would be equitably dealt with and judged according to their knowledge.

What answers the objection from antiquity and numbers. Calvin sets out the two lets, long antiquity of time and the consent of almost all nations, and answers that an eternal truth cannot be prescribed against by length of years nor kept off by the conspiracy of the world; Wesley makes the same answer in a sentence, that the multitude of them that err does not turn error into truth, and supplies the objection itself, that the hearers might say they would have heard it from their fathers.

Why the rain in particular. Barnes argues from the untraceability of its laws, as against the fixed laws of sun and stars, that it seems poured directly from God's hollow hand; Robertson notes that Zeus was the god of rain and Lycaonia often dry, so the item was well chosen; Calvin argues from the regular order of the seasons that heaven and earth are not moved by their own motion nor by fortune; Clarke finds the evidence in the measure rather than the fact, God giving neither less than is necessary nor more than is sufficient.
outliers: Ellicott alone hears a quotation in the closing words, judging them so distinctly rhythmical that Paul may be repeating a hymn heard at a harvest or vintage festival and claiming it, as he claimed the altar to the Unknown God, for the God men ignorantly worshipped.
Ellicott alone observes that the argument is fitted to the audience, nature for peasants at Lystra and conscience for philosophers at Athens and Rome.
Clarke alone reads providence as a balance rather than a gift, arguing that by not giving too much God prevents luxury and riot and by giving enough prevents discontent and misery.
Calvin alone answers the objection that men more often mourn from hunger than rejoice from plenty, replying that this happens contrary to the order of nature.
themes: suffered all nations to walk in their own ways
he left not himself without witness
rain from heaven and fruitful seasons
filling our hearts with food and gladness

18.pericope_label: And with these sayings scarce restrained they the people, that they had not done sacrifice unto them. And there came thither certain Jews from Antioch and Iconium, who persuaded the people, and, having stoned Paul, drew him out of the city, supposing he had been dead.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the barely restrained crowd and the reversal. Gill says with these sayings means the words concerning themselves, and concerning the living God, his creation of all things, and his providential goodness. On the next verse Gill says there came thither certain Jews either just at the same time or while the apostles were in the city, and that in four manuscripts and some other copies it is read, as they abode there and taught, there came; these Jews were inveterate enemies of the apostles and seemed to have followed them from place to place on purpose to oppose them, to stir up the people against them, and to hinder the success of their ministry all they could. Calvin says Luke said before that they did not only use words but ran also with violence into the multitude, and now adds that the fury of the people was scarce repressed with that vehemency, whereby appeareth how mad and untamed the heat of the world is toward idolatry. For if they believe them gods, Calvin asks, why do they not believe their word, whereby they put from them false honour? But all idolaters are sick of this disease, that they are oftentimes ready to shake off the yoke unless religion be subject to their will and pleasure; wherefore no marvel if the prophets say oftentimes that men are carried into the blind affection of superstitions, even as brute beasts are carried into their lust. On the next verse Calvin says Paul and Barnabas can hardly stay the people from doing sacrifice, but a company of knaves do with small ado persuade them to stone Paul, whom of late they made a god, whereby appeareth how much more men be bent unto superstition than unto the true worship of God, and how arrogant superstition is, which will always bear the chief sway in appointing the worship of God. The servants of God seek no other thing but to bring men under obedience of him, which is salvation and felicity alone, Calvin says: they challenge to themselves no lordship, they hunt after no gain, and yet the world cannot abide them; while those who are thus stubborn against God are too ready to believe seducers, and willingly submit themselves to their tyranny. In this history is most lively painted out unto us the forwardness of the world, Calvin says: Paul might have reigned under the title of Mercury, with the commendation of all men; he will not be a god; because he serveth Christ faithfully, he is stoned. His constancy is commended, to the end we may follow it. He was indeed wonderfully delivered by the Lord, but as touching himself he suffered a most cruel kind of death; therefore we must make like account of this testimony, which he doth also recite in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, as if he had been slain. We need not doubt but that the mob rose tumultuously against him, Calvin adds, so that whatsoever violence the wicked do to the servants of Christ is never called in question: the laws are silent, judgments cease, the magistrate is asleep, and there is no patron to be found.

Henry takes the incensing of the people and the deliverance. We have here a further account of the services and sufferings of Paul and Barnabas, Henry says, and first how Paul was stoned and left for dead but miraculously came to himself again. They fell upon Paul rather than Barnabas because Paul, being the chief speaker, galled and vexed them more than Barnabas did. The people were incensed against Paul not by any injury they pretended he had done them, Henry says, for if they took it for an affront that he would not let them misplace divine honours upon him, when they considered themselves they would easily forgive him that wrong; but there came certain Jews from Antioch, hearing and vexed to hear what respect was shown to Paul and Barnabas at Lystra, and they incensed the people against them as factious, seditious, dangerous persons, not fit to be harboured. See how restless the rage of the Jews was against the gospel of Christ, Henry says: they could not bear that it should have footing anywhere. They were irritated to such a degree that the mob rose and stoned Paul, not by a judicial sentence but in a popular tumult; they threw stones at him, with which they knocked him down, and then drew him out of the city as one not fit to live in it, or drew him out in a cart to bury him, supposing he had been dead. So strong is the bias of the corrupt and carnal heart to that which is evil, Henry says, that as it is with great difficulty that men are restrained from evil on one side, so it is with great ease that they are persuaded to evil on the other. See how fickle and mutable the minds of carnal worldly people are: those that but the other day would have treated the apostles as more than men now treat them as worse than brutes, as the worst of malefactors. Today Hosanna, tomorrow Crucify; today sacrificed to, tomorrow sacrificed. We have an instance of a change the other way later in this book, where the same man is first a murderer and then no doubt a god. Popular breath turns like the wind, Henry says. If Paul would have been Mercury, he might have been enthroned, nay, he might have been enshrined; but if he will be a faithful minister of Christ, he shall be stoned and thrown out of the city; thus those who easily submit to strong delusions hate to receive the truth in the love of it. When he was drawn out of the city the disciples stood round about him, Henry says: it seems there were some here at Lystra that became disciples, that found the mean between deifying the apostles and rejecting them, and even these new converts had courage to own Paul when he was thus run down, though they had reason to fear that the same that stoned him would stone them for owning him. They stood round about him as a guard against the further outrage of the people, and to see whether he were alive or dead, and all of a sudden he rose up. Though he was not dead, Henry says, yet he was ill crushed and bruised, no doubt, and fainted away; he was in a swoon, so that it was not without a miracle that he came so soon to himself and was so well as to be able to go into the city. God's faithful servants, though they may be brought within a step of death and may be looked upon as dead both by friends and enemies, shall not die as long as he has work for them to do: they are cast down, but not destroyed.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the restraint, the distance travelled and the stoning. Barnes says the arguments scarce restrained the people, who were so fully satisfied that the gods had appeared and were so full of zeal to do them honour. On the next verse he says that, not satisfied with having expelled them from Antioch and Iconium, they still pursued them: persecutors often exhibit a zeal and perseverance in a bad cause which it would be well if Christians evinced in a holy cause, and men will often travel farther to do evil than they will to do good, many showing more zeal in opposing the gospel than professed Christians do in advancing it. They stoned Paul, whom they were just before ready to worship as a god, Barnes says: what a striking instance of the fickleness and instability of idolaters, and what a striking instance of the instability and uselessness of mere popularity. Just before, they were ready to adore him; now they sought to put him to death; nothing is more fickle than mere popular favour, and the unbounded admiration of a man may soon be changed into unbounded indignation and contempt. It was well for Paul that he was not seeking this popularity and did not depend on it for happiness, Barnes says: he had a good conscience, he was engaged in a good cause, he was under the protection of God, and his happiness was to be sought from a higher source than the applause of men. They drew him out of the city probably in haste and in popular rage, as if he was unfit to be in the city and unworthy of a decent burial, for it does not appear that they contemplated an interment, but indignantly dragged him beyond the walls to leave him there. The next verse shows that he was really not dead, Barnes says, though many commentators, as well as the Jews, have supposed that he was and was miraculously restored to life; and it is remarkable that Barnabas was not exposed to this popular fury, but it is to be remembered that Paul was the chief speaker and it was his peculiar zeal that exposed him. Ellicott says that on some of those who were thus restrained the effect may well have been that they were roused to a higher life and did turn from vanities to the living God, and that we must think of Paul's work at Lystra as lasting long enough to allow time for the foundation of a church there. Among the more conspicuous converts were the devout Jewesses Lois and her daughter Eunice, and the young Timotheus, Ellicott says; no mention is made of his father, and Eunice may have been a widow, but the fact that the boy had grown up uncircumcised rather suggests the influence of a living father. On the next verse Ellicott says the context shows that the Pisidian Antioch is meant, and that the strength of the hostility is shown by the facts that the Jews of the two cities were acting in concert and that those of the former had travelled not less than a hundred and thirty miles to hinder the Apostle's work. The sudden change of feeling is almost as startling as that which transformed the hosannas of the multitudes at Jerusalem into the cry of Crucify him, Ellicott says, but it is not difficult to understand these vicissitudes of feeling in a barbarous and superstitious people, and we find a like sudden change in an opposite direction in the people of Melita: if the strangers endowed with such mysterious powers were not gods in the likeness of men, they might be sorcerers or even demons, and the Jews, ever ready to impute signs and wonders to Beelzebub, would readily work on this feeling and terrify the people into the cruel ferocity of panic. The mode of punishment shows that it was planned and executed by Jews, Ellicott says: they were apparently eager to satisfy themselves that they were inflicting punishment on a blasphemer, stoning him to death and casting him out to be buried with the burial of an ass; and so, in one sense, as from man's way of looking on such things, the martyr expiated the guilt of the persecutor, the blinding, stunning blows falling on him as they had fallen on Stephen. It was the one instance in Paul's life of this form of suffering, and the sufferings endured at Lystra stand out at the close of his life in the vista of past years with a marvellous distinctness. Robertson notes that scarce is an adverb from a word for toil, that restrained is an effective aorist of an old verb in the causative sense to make abstain from, and that it had been a harrowing and well-nigh a horrible ordeal, but finally Paul had won — if only nobody else had interposed. On the next verse he says whether news of the miracle had reached those cities we do not know, and that these may have been travelling grain merchants; at any rate there was an interval in which Paul and Barnabas won some disciples, and there would be a natural reaction, even revulsion, in the minds of many who had come so near to worshipping them, since the pendulum swings easily from one extreme to the other. The hostile Jews from Antioch and Iconium may even have followed Paul and Barnabas along the fine Roman road on purpose to keep them on the run, Robertson says; they had driven them out of Antioch and out of Iconium and now appear at Lystra at an opportune moment for their work, having complete success with many and striking at the psychological moment. They stoned Paul as the chief speaker, Mercury, and passed by Barnabas, Jupiter; it was a Jewish mode of punishment as against Stephen, and these Jews knew that Paul was the man they had to deal with. The wounds inflicted may have left some of the scars mentioned in Galatians, Robertson adds, and a commentator notes that the Jews with two exceptions incited the persecutions which Paul endured, the exceptions being Philippi and Ephesus. They hurled Stephen outside of the city before stoning him, and it was a hurried and irregular proceeding, but they were dragging Paul out now. The Jews are jubilant this time with memories of Paul's escape at Antioch and Iconium, Robertson says, and the pagan mob feel that they have settled accounts for their narrow escape from worshipping two Jewish renegade preachers: it was a good day's work for them all. Luke does not say that Paul was actually dead.

Clarke and Wesley take the pursuit and the fickleness. There came thither certain Jews from Antioch, Clarke says, and these were no doubt the same who had raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas at Iconium and Antioch before: they followed the apostles with implacable malice, and what they could not do themselves they endeavoured to do by others, whose minds they first perverted and then irritated to deeds of fell purpose. Alas, of what real worth is popular fame, Clarke asks; how uncertain, and how unworthy to be counted. These poor heathens acted just like the people of Malta: when the viper fastened on the hand of Paul they concluded he was a murderer, and when they found it did him no damage they changed their minds and said he was a god; when the Lycaonians saw the miracles that Paul did they said he was the god Mercury, and when the persecuting Jews came they persuaded them that he was an impostor, and then they endeavoured to stone him to death. They did not leave stoning him till they had the fullest evidence that he was dead, Clarke says, and so, most probably, he was. Wesley says of the words who persuaded the multitude that they were moved with equal ease either to adore or murder him.

debates: Whether Paul actually died. Clarke says they did not leave off stoning until they had the fullest evidence of death, and so most probably he was dead; Barnes says the next verse shows he was not, though many commentators and the Jews supposed he was and was miraculously restored to life; Robertson notes only that Luke does not say he was actually dead; Henry has him not dead but crushed and swooning, so that his recovery was still a miracle; Calvin says the account must be kept as a death, since as touching himself he suffered a most cruel kind of death.

Why the crowd turned. Ellicott explains it by the vicissitudes of feeling natural to a barbarous and superstitious people, who, if the strangers were not gods, might take them for sorcerers or demons, the Jews working on that fear; Robertson calls it a natural reaction and revulsion after coming so near to worship; Calvin makes it evidence that men are more bent to superstition than to true worship; Henry sees the bias of the carnal heart, hard to restrain from evil on one side and easy to persuade to it on the other.

Whether Timothy's father was living. Ellicott says no mention is made of him and Eunice may have been a widow, but that the boy's having grown up uncircumcised rather suggests the influence of a living father; Robertson, at the earlier verse, supposes Eunice possibly a widow living with her mother Lois.

How the Jews came to be there. Ellicott has them travelling not less than a hundred and thirty miles from the Pisidian Antioch and acting in concert with those of Iconium; Robertson allows that they may have been travelling grain merchants who happened on the moment, or may have followed along the Roman road on purpose to keep the apostles on the run; Gill says they seemed to have followed from place to place to hinder the ministry all they could; Barnes turns it into a reproach, that men will travel farther to do evil than to do good.
outliers: Six of them independently strike the same antithesis on the reversal, Henry with today Hosanna, tomorrow Crucify, Calvin with Paul refusing to reign under the title of Mercury and being stoned for serving Christ, Barnes with the uselessness of mere popularity, Robertson with the swinging pendulum, Wesley with moved with equal ease either to adore or murder him.
Henry, Clarke and Ellicott all reach independently for the islanders of Melita, who took Paul first for a murderer and then for a god, as the same reversal run backwards.
Ellicott alone reads the stoning as a settling of accounts, that the blinding blows fell on Paul as they had fallen on Stephen, so that in one sense the martyr expiated the guilt of the persecutor.
Ellicott alone looks past the mob to the church it left behind, counting Lois, Eunice and the young Timothy among the converts of a stay long enough to found one.
themes: drew him out of the city

20.pericope_label: Howbeit, as the disciples stood round about him, he rose up, and came into the city: and the next day he departed with Barnabas to Derbe. And when they had preached the gospel to that city, and had taught many, they returned again to Lystra, and to Iconium, and Antioch,

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the circle of disciples and the miracle. Gill says the disciples stood round about him, weeping over him and lamenting for him, and it may be praying to God that he would restore him to life; however, they got about him in order to take care of him and provide for his interment. These were the young converts at Lystra who under the ministry of the apostles were now brought to the faith of Christ, Gill says, unless it can be thought that they were such as followed them from other places, but the former seems most probable, and it shows their affection to their spiritual Father and their constancy in the faith of Christ notwithstanding this ill treatment of his servant. On the next verse Gill says they preached the Gospel to the inhabitants of that city, as they did in every place where they came, even the pure Gospel of Christ, the good news and glad tidings of life and salvation by him. Calvin says that though no man defended Paul, yet Luke showeth that the godly were anxious for his life, yet they did so moderate themselves lest they should attempt anything with great danger to no end, seeing they could not help him unless it were done privily. We must always mark what the Lord hath brought to our hand, Calvin says: if I, standing upon the bank, shall see a man in the midst of the water and cannot reach him my hand when he is like to be drowned, what is remaining for me to do but to commend him to the Lord? But if there be any hope to help him, then must I run the risk. Therefore we will not say that Paul was left alone by the disciples through sloth, seeing they could not help him, and they declare their love and care when they stand about him after he is cast out. It appeareth plainly by this that Paul was miraculously saved, Calvin says, seeing that on the morrow, after he was cast out for dead, he taketh his journey being fresh and sound; whence it is also gathered what an invincible heart he bare against all evils and afflictions, for he creepeth not into a corner where, like an overworn soldier, he may live idly, but he goeth to the same places where he was uncourteously and cruelly handled but a little before. Notwithstanding Luke showeth that the church was first planted among the men of Derbe, Calvin says, he addeth afterward that Paul and Barnabas returned unto the churches which they had ordained that they might confirm the disciples, whereby he giveth us to understand that the use of the Word consisteth not in instruction only, whereby the hearer is only taught, but that it is also available for confirmation of faith, in admonishing, exhorting and reproving. Christ doth not only command his ministers to teach but also to exhort, and Paul saith that the Scripture is profitable not only to teach but also to exhort; wherefore let not pastors think that they have done their duty as they ought when they have well trained up their people in true knowledge, unless they employ themselves to this part also, and let not the faithful neglect the Word of God, because there is no man who hath not need of continual confirmation.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the recovery, the distance to Derbe and the courage of the return. Barnes says that notwithstanding the supposition that he was dead, it would seem the disciples did not suppose him dead but might be expecting that he would revive. Most commentators have supposed that his rising was the effect of a miracle, Barnes says, maintaining that he could not have risen so soon and entered into the city without the interposition of miraculous power, and he names Calvin, Doddridge and Clarke among them; but the commentators have asserted that which is not intimated by the sacred penman, and there is no propriety in supposing the intervention of miraculous agency where it is not necessary. The probability is that he was stunned by a blow, perhaps a single blow, and after a short time recovered from it, Barnes says: nothing is more common than thus by a violent blow on the head to be rendered apparently lifeless, the effect of which is soon over and the person restored to strength; and two other scholars suppose that Paul feigned himself to be dead and rose when out of danger. It is remarkable that he should have returned again to the same city, Barnes says, but probably it was only among the new converts that he showed himself, the Jews supposing that he was dead; and the opposition was such that it was vain to attempt to preach there any longer, so that, having been seen by the disciples after his supposed death, their faith was confirmed and he departed to preach in another place. On the next verse Barnes says had taught many is rather had made many disciples, and that we have here a remarkable instance of the courage of the apostles: in these very places they had been persecuted and stoned, and yet in the face of danger they ventured to return, the welfare of the infant churches being deemed of more consequence than their own safety, and they threw themselves again into the midst of danger to comfort and strengthen those just converted to God. There are times when ministers should not count their own lives dear to them, Barnes says, but should fearlessly throw themselves into the midst of danger, confiding only in the protecting care of their God and Saviour. Ellicott says the disciples had been powerless to prevent the attack, but they stole out when all was over, it may be with the purpose of giving at least a decent interment, and we may fairly think of Lois and Eunice and Timotheus as present in that crowd, weeping first for sorrow and then for exceeding joy to find that the teacher whom they loved was stunned only, and not dead. The journey to Derbe must have occupied several hours, Ellicott says, and we do well to remember that after the suffering of the previous day it must have been one of peculiar hardship and fatigue; the city was twenty miles to the east of Lystra, just within the Cappadocian boundary of Isauria, and the exact site has not been identified, though the ruins of an acropolis have been found not far from a lake which have been supposed to be the remains of Derbe. The whole region was infamous for its brigandage, Ellicott adds, and there may be a reference to this in the perils of robbers of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians. On the next verse he says had taught many is better made many disciples, the word being the same as in the great commission, and among these we may note Gaius, afterwards conspicuous as one of Paul's companions; the work done implies a stay of, it may be, some months' duration, during which the violence of the hostility of the Jews at Antioch and Iconium had probably subsided, so that the Apostles could revisit those cities, as they retraced their steps, without any great danger. Robertson says the would-be murderers left and a group of disciples gathered round to see if Paul was dead or alive and, if dead, to bury him, and that in that group Timothy may very well have been along with Eunice and Barnabas: Timothy, a lad of about fifteen, would not soon forget that solemn scene. But Paul suddenly, apparently a miraculous recovery, rose up and entered the city to the surprise and joy of the disciples who were willing to brave persecution with him, Robertson says; it was plainly unwise to continue in Lystra, so they set out on the next day, shaken and bruised as Paul was, Derbe being some forty miles distant, near the pass to the Cilician Gates. On the next verse Robertson says they evangelized that city, a smaller city and apparently with no trouble from the Jews, and that had made many disciples uses a late verb meaning to make a disciple as in the great commission: Paul and Barnabas were literally here obeying the command of Jesus in discipling people in this heathen city. Derbe was the frontier city of the Roman empire, and the quickest way to return to Antioch in Syria would have been by the Cilician Gates or by the pass over Mount Taurus, but difficult to travel in winter; it was necessary to revisit the churches in Lystra, Iconium and Antioch in Pisidia and to see that they were able to withstand persecution. Paul was a Roman citizen though he had not made use of this privilege as yet for his own protection, Robertson notes: against mob violence it would count for little, but he did not hesitate; he had been stoned in Lystra, threatened in Iconium, expelled in Antioch, and he shows his wisdom in conserving his work.

Clarke and Wesley take the prayer of the disciples and the manner of the stoning. The disciples stood round about him no doubt in earnest prayer, Clarke says, entreating the Author of life that his soul might again return to its battered tenement; he rose up miraculously restored, not only to life but to perfect soundness, so that he was able to walk into the city, that his persecutors might see the mighty power of God in his restoration and the faith of the young converts be confirmed in the truth and goodness of God. It is strange that neither the young converts at Lystra nor Barnabas were involved in this persecution, Clarke adds: it seems to have had Paul alone for its object, and when they thought they had despatched him they did not think of injuring the rest. On the next verse Clarke says, behold the courage of these Christian men: they counted not their lives dear to them, and returned to do their Master's work in the very places in which they had been so grievously persecuted, and where one of them had been apparently stoned to death; the man who knows he is God's ambassador, and that his life depends on his fidelity to his Master, knows he has nothing but his God to fear. Wesley says the disciples stood round probably after sunset, since the enraged multitude would scarce have suffered it in the day time, and that his rising and going into the city, just after he had been left for dead, was a miracle little less than a resurrection from the dead, especially considering the manner wherein the Jewish malefactors were stoned: the witnesses first threw as large a stone as they could lift, with all possible violence, upon his head, which alone was sufficient to dash the skull in pieces, and all the people then joined, as long as any motion or token of life remained.

debates: Whether the recovery was miraculous. Barnes denies it, holding that there is no propriety in supposing miraculous agency where it is not necessary and that Paul was probably stunned by a single blow, and he names Calvin and Clarke among the commentators who have asserted what the sacred penman does not intimate; Calvin says it appeareth plainly that Paul was miraculously saved, since he took his journey next day fresh and sound; Clarke says he was restored not only to life but to perfect soundness; Wesley calls it a miracle little less than a resurrection and argues it from the Jewish manner of stoning; Robertson calls it apparently a miraculous recovery; Ellicott stands with Barnes, that Paul was stunned only and not dead.

Whether the return to the hostile cities was brave or safe. Barnes calls it a remarkable instance of courage and says the apostles threw themselves again into the midst of danger; Clarke says behold the courage of these Christian men, who counted not their lives dear; Robertson makes it necessary work in conserving the churches, and notes that Paul's Roman citizenship would have counted for little against mob violence; Ellicott reckons that a stay of some months at Derbe had let the hostility subside, so that they could retrace their steps without any great danger.

How far Derbe lay from Lystra. Ellicott makes it twenty miles to the east, just within the Cappadocian boundary, with the exact site unidentified; Robertson makes it some forty miles, near the pass to the Cilician Gates; both agree the journey came the day after the stoning, Ellicott adding that it must have been one of peculiar hardship and fatigue.

What the disciples standing round were doing. Gill has them weeping and lamenting and perhaps praying that God would restore him to life; Clarke has them in earnest prayer for his soul's return; Ellicott has them come out to give at least a decent interment; Robertson has them gathered to see whether he was dead or alive and, if dead, to bury him; Barnes alone says they do not seem to have supposed him dead at all.
outliers: Barnes alone argues against a miracle here, and does it by naming two commentators whose notes stand in this same catena, saying they have asserted what the sacred penman does not intimate.

Wesley alone supplies the forensic detail, describing how the witnesses threw the first and largest stone upon the head with all possible violence, enough of itself to dash the skull in pieces, and how the people then joined in as long as any token of life remained.
Clarke alone notices who was not attacked, finding it strange that neither Barnabas nor the young converts were touched, so that the persecution seems to have had Paul alone for its object.
Ellicott alone connects the road to Derbe with the perils of robbers Paul afterwards lists, the whole region being infamous for brigandage.

he rose up and came into the city
