22.pericope_label: Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God. And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the confirming and the manner of ordaining. Gill says they confirmed not wicked men in their wickedness, nor self-righteous persons in an opinion of their own righteousness, both being contrary to the tendency of the ministry of the word, but the disciples and followers of Jesus whom they had already made in those places, confirming them in the doctrines of the Gospel and fortifying them against the contradictions and blasphemies of the Jews and the persecutions they met with. They did not confirm the bodies of these disciples and the health of them, Gill says, which is the business of the physician to confirm, nor their estates and civil property, to secure and defend which belongs to the civil magistrate, but their souls, their more noble and valuable part, their hearts, which are apt to be unstable. On the next verse Gill says that as soon as ever any number of disciples were made in any place they were at once formed by the apostles into a church state, and that among those converted there were some honoured with ministerial gifts qualifying them to preach the Gospel and take the care of the churches: these the apostles directed the churches to look out from among themselves, as in the case of deacons, who by joint suffrages declared their choice of them by the stretching out or lifting up of their hands, as the word here used signifies, and not the imposition of them; and the apostles presiding in this affair, they were installed into the office of bishops, elders or pastors over them. Calvin says the principal way to confirm was that they provoked the disciples who had before embraced the Gospel to go forward by exhorting them, for we are far from being so prompt as we ought: our laziness needeth pricks and our coldness must be warmed. But because God will have his exercised with diverse combats, Calvin says, Paul and Barnabas admonish the disciples to be ready to suffer tribulation, a very necessary admonition, that we must go on warfare in this world that we may live well and godly. If the flesh should not molest us, if Satan should attempt nothing, if the wicked should not trouble us, it were no such troublesome thing to persevere, for that were a sweet walk through a pleasant way; but because there arise on every side and every moment infinite assaults which provoke us to fall away, there ariseth the difficulty, and therefore is it that the virtue of constancy is so rare, so that to the end we may persist even unto the end we must be prepared for war. Luke speaketh not in this place only of the persecutions which the adversaries raise against us with drawn swords and flaming fires, Calvin says, but comprehendeth under the word all sorrows and miseries whereunto the life of the godly is subject; not because the faithful alone are miserable, since this is the common state both of the good and the bad, whence also cometh that famous proverb, that it is best not to be born and the next best to die very quickly. But when God doth oftentimes spare the wicked and doth fat them with prosperity, he is more harsh toward his children: besides common molestations they are oppressed peculiarly with many discommodities, and the Lord doth humble them with such exercises, keeping their flesh under correction lest it wax wanton. Unto these are added the reproaches and slanders of the wicked, Calvin says, for they must be as it were the offscourings of the world; and last of all the lust of the wicked breaketh out into open violence, so that all their life shall be unquiet amidst so many enemies. But this is the best comfort, and sufficient to confirm their minds, that this way, though it be hard and sharp, leadeth unto the kingdom of heaven; for we gather by this that the miseries of the godly are more happy than all the delights of the world. On the next verse Calvin says it is not enough if men have been once taught the doctrine of godliness unless they go forward continually, and therefore Christ did not only send his apostles to preach the gospel but commanded also that there should be pastors appointed, that the preaching of the gospel might be perpetual and in daily use. Paul and Barnabas mark that this order was set down by Christ when they assign pastors to every church, Calvin says, lest after their departure doctrine should cease and be silent; and this place teacheth that the Church cannot want an ordinary ministry, neither can any be counted Christians before God but those who during their whole life are willing to learn. I take it that those are called elders in this place who had the office of teaching enjoined them, Calvin says, for it appeareth by Paul that some were only censors of manners; and forasmuch as Luke saith that they were set over every church, the difference between their office and the office of the apostles is gathered hence, for the apostles had no certain place of abode but went to and fro to found new churches, while pastors were set and appointed, every man to his own church, and were as it were placed as a guard over their congregations. The Greek word doth signify to decree or ordain a thing by lifting up the hands, as they used to do in the assemblies of the people, Calvin says, notwithstanding the ecclesiastical writers do often use the word in another sense, for the solemn rite of ordaining. By this manner of speech is very excellently expressed the right way to ordain pastors: Paul and Barnabas are said to elect elders. Do they this alone by their peculiar office? Nay, rather they suffer the matter to be decided by the suffrages of them all; therefore in ordaining pastors the people had their free election, but lest there should any tumult arise, Paul and Barnabas sit as chief moderators. Thus must the decree of the council of Laodicea be understood, which forbiddeth that election be left to the people. They had a double end and reason of their prayer, Calvin says: the first, that God would direct them with the spirit of wisdom and discretion to choose the best and most meet men, for they knew that they were not furnished with so great wisdom but they might be deceived, neither did they so much trust to their diligence but that they knew the principal point did consist in the blessing of God.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the word confirming, the sense of the faith, the pronoun we, and the mode of appointment. Barnes says the expression to confirm has in some churches a technical signification, denoting to admit to the full privileges of a Christian by the imposition of hands, and that the word here refers to no such rite: it has no reference to any imposition of hands, nor to the thing usually supposed to be denoted by the rite of confirmation, but means simply that they established, strengthened, made firm or encouraged by the presentation of truth and by the motives of the gospel. Whether the rite of confirmation as practised by some churches be founded on the authority of the New Testament or not, Barnes says, it is certain that it can receive no support from this passage; the truth was that these were young converts, surrounded by enemies, exposed to temptations, with but a slight acquaintance with the truths of the gospel, and there is not the slightest evidence that they had not been admitted to the full privileges of the church before, or that any ceremony was now performed. On the words that we must, Barnes says the meaning is that it is fit or proper that we should, not that it is in itself fixed by any fatal necessity, but that such is the nature of religion and such the wickedness and opposition of the world that it will happen; we are not to expect that it will be otherwise, and we are to calculate on it when we become Christians. It is proper, he says, because such is the opposition of the world to pure religion that it cannot be avoided, of which they had striking demonstration in Lystra and Iconium; because it is necessary to reclaim us from wandering and to keep us in the path of duty; because it is necessary to wean us from the world, trial here making us pant for a world of rest; and because when we are persecuted we may remember that it has been the lot of Christians from the beginning, since we tread a path watered by the tears of the saints. On the next verse Barnes says the word ordain we now use in an ecclesiastical sense, to denote a setting apart to an office by the imposition of hands, but it is evident that the word here is not employed in that sense: it occurs but in one other place in the New Testament, where it is applied to Luke and translated chosen of the church, that is, appointed or elected by suffrage. The verb properly denotes to stretch out the hand, Barnes says, and as it was customary to elect to office or to vote by stretching out or elevating the hand, the word simply means to elect, appoint or designate to any office; it refers here simply to an election or appointment of the elders. It is said that Paul and Barnabas did this, he says, but probably all that is meant is that they presided in the assembly when the choice was made: it does not mean that they appointed them without consulting the church, but it evidently means that they appointed them in the usual way of appointing officers, by the suffrages of the people. Elders is literally presbyters, a word relating to the aged but also to office, denoting those more experienced than others, to preside over and instruct the rest; all that seems implied is that they were to take the charge of the churches during the absence of the apostles, and the probability is that they performed all the functions required in the infant churches, in exhorting, instructing and governing. Ellicott says confirming is better rendered strengthening, so as to avoid the more definite associations connected with the other term, and that it is not the same word as that used by later writers for the ecclesiastical rite of Confirmation. The question meets us whether faith is used in its subjective sense, the feeling of trust, or objectively as including the main substance of what was believed and taught, a belief or creed, Ellicott says, and that the latter meaning had become established a few years after Luke wrote we see in the epistles, so that on the whole it seems probable that it is so used here. The use of the first personal pronoun is suggestive, he says: is Luke generalising what he heard from those who had listened to Paul, and giving it in their very words? Was he himself one of those listeners? The two had clearly met before we find them both at Troas. In Paul's latest epistle to the chosen disciple of Lystra we have a touching reproduction of this teaching, Ellicott adds, where he speaks of the afflictions which came on him at Antioch, at Iconium, at Lystra, and adds the general truth that all who will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecutions. We may pause to note the occurrence of the familiar phrase and thought of the Gospels, the kingdom of God, in the earliest recorded teaching of Paul, Ellicott says: for him too that which was proclaimed was not a theory or an opinion but an actual kingdom, of which Jesus the Christ was king. On the next verse Ellicott says the word for ordained occurs in the New Testament here and in one other place, where it is translated chosen, and certainly seems to imply popular election by show of hands, which is indeed the natural meaning of the word; but used, as it is here, of the act of the two Apostles, not of the Church, the meaning of appointment seems most in harmony with the context. There may have been a previous election, or the names of those to be appointed may have been submitted to the approval of the Church, Ellicott says, but the word cannot in itself be held to imply either. It is interesting to note that Paul and Barnabas, by virtue of the authority which as Apostles they had received primarily from Christ and mediately from the Church of Antioch, exercised the right of appointing, or in later phrase ordaining, elders; that they plant among the Churches of the Gentiles the organisation found at Jerusalem, itself based on that of the Synagogue and not on that of the Temple; that as this appears as the first appointment it would seem to follow that the disciples had in the meantime met, and taught, and baptised, and broken bread without them, organisation of this kind being important for the permanence of the life of the Church but not essential to its being, or to the spiritual growth of individual members; and that the elders so appointed were the same as those known in the Apostolic Church as bishops or overseers. It is a legitimate inference from the recurrence of the act, Ellicott adds, that Paul and Barnabas recognised prayer and fasting as an established rule of the Church in preparation for the solemn work of appointing men to spiritual functions: without prayer such an appointment was a mockery, and fasting served to intensify prayer. The word rendered commended implies the confiding trust of one who commits what is very precious to him to the keeping of another. Robertson says confirming is a late verb found in the New Testament only in Acts, meaning to make more firm, to give additional strength, and used each time concerning these churches. It is possible that faith here has the notion of creed as Paul uses it later, he says, and it seems to be here more than trust or belief, since these recent converts from heathenism were ill-informed, were persecuted, had broken family and social ties, and greatly needed encouragement if they were to hold out. It does not follow from this use of we that Luke was present, Robertson insists, since it is a general proposition applying to all Christians at all times, though Luke of course approved the principle; a scholar asks why Timothy may not have told Luke about Paul's work, and it all sounds like quotation of Paul's very language. On the next verse Robertson says the verb from stretching out the hand originally meant to vote by show of hands, finally to appoint with the approval of an assembly that chooses, and then to appoint without regard to choice; the seven at Jerusalem were first selected by the church and then appointed by the apostles, and that is probably the plan contemplated by Paul in his directions to Titus and the one pursued here: they selected the elders in each instance and Paul and Barnabas ordained them, as we say, though the word does not mean that. It is fairly certain that these elders were chosen to correspond in a general way with the elders in the Jewish synagogue, after which the local church was largely copied as to organisation and worship, Robertson says; the use of the plural implies that each church had its college of elders, elder being the Jewish name and bishop the Greek name for the same office, and teaching was a normal function of these elders. It was a serious matter, this formal setting apart, so it was done in a public meeting with prayer and fasting, and the word for commended is an old and solemn word, to entrust, to deposit as in a bank.

Clarke and Wesley take the school of the Church, the standard of doctrine and the two Greek words. The word disciple signifies literally a scholar, Clarke says: the Church of Christ was a school in which Christ himself was chief Master and his apostles subordinate teachers, and all the converts were scholars who came to this school to be instructed in the knowledge of themselves and of their God. After having been initiated in the principles of the heavenly doctrine they needed line upon line and precept upon precept, in order that they might be confirmed and established in the truth, Clarke says; and though it was a great and important thing to have their understanding properly informed, yet if the heart was not disciplined, information in the understanding would be of little avail, therefore they confirmed the souls of the disciples. As there must be some particular standard of truth to which they might continually resort, it was necessary that they should have such a system of doctrine as they knew came from God, Clarke says, and these doctrines, containing all the essential principles of Christianity, were called The Faith; and as the spirit of the world would be ever opposed to the spirit of Christ, they must make up their minds to expect persecution and therefore had need of confirmed souls and strong faith. As the mind must faint under trouble that sees no prospect of its termination, it was necessary that they should keep in view the kingdom of God, and they were informed that these tribulations were the very means which God would use to bring them into his own kingdom. On the next verse Clarke says elder seems to be here the name of an office: these were all young or new converts, and yet among them the apostles constitute elders, appointing persons the most experienced and the most advanced in the divine life to watch over and instruct the rest. But what is the meaning of the word we translate ordained, Clarke asks. We use ordain in an ecclesiastical sense, signifying the appointment of a person to an office in the Church by the imposition of the hands of those who are rulers in that Church; but the one Greek word signifies the holding up or stretching out of the hand, as approving of the choice of any person to a particular work, whereas the other signifies the imposition of hands. Clarke quotes an old canonist at length, that nowadays a course of prayers and invocation of the Holy Spirit when one is initiated into the priesthood is called by the first word, so termed because the bishop extends his hand over him whom he blesses; but anciently the choice or suffrage was called by that word, for when it was lawful for the multitude in their cities to choose their priests or bishops they met together, and that it might appear whose suffrage won they stretched forth their hands and were so numbered, and him who was elected by the most suffrages they placed in the high priesthood. I believe the simple truth to be this, Clarke concludes, that in ancient times the people chose by the stretching out of hands their spiritual pastor, and the rulers of the Church, whether apostles or others, appointed that person to his office by the imposition of hands, and perhaps each of these was thought to be equally necessary. Having prayed with fasting was to implore God's special assistance, as they well knew that without his influence even their appointment could avail nothing, and commended them to the Lord means to his especial care and protection. Wesley says they ordained presbyters in every Church out of those who were themselves but newly converted: so soon can God enable even a babe in Christ to build up others in the common faith; and they commended them to the Lord, an expression implying faith in Christ as well as love to the brethren.

debates: What the word rendered ordained implies. Barnes says the verb properly means to stretch out the hand and therefore simply to elect, so that Paul and Barnabas presided while the church chose by suffrage; Gill has the churches look out men from among themselves and declare their choice by lifting up the hand, and not by the imposition of it; Clarke separates the stretching out of hands in election from the laying on of hands in appointment and thinks both were required; Calvin asks whether the two did it by their private office and answers that the people had their free election while the apostles sat as chief moderators; Robertson allows the verb had come to mean appointment without regard to choice, but thinks the churches selected and the apostles ordained; Ellicott alone, granting that popular election is the natural sense of the word, sets it aside because the verb is used here of the Apostles and not of the Church.

Whether the faith is trust or creed. Ellicott states the alternative and judges the objective sense probable, since it was established a few years after Luke wrote; Robertson says it seems here more than trust or belief; Clarke assumes it throughout, arguing that a standard of doctrine known to come from God was needed and was called The Faith.

What the pronoun in we must implies about Luke. Ellicott finds it suggestive and asks whether Luke was himself among Paul's hearers, noting that the two had met before Troas; Robertson denies that anything follows, since the sentence is a general proposition true of all Christians at all times, and adds that Timothy might have told Luke about the work.

What confirming means. Barnes denies it any reference to the later rite of imposition of hands and says the passage can give that rite no support; Ellicott prefers strengthening in order to avoid the association and notes that the Greek is not the word later writers use of the rite; Robertson takes it simply as giving additional strength; Gill defines it by exclusion, not the body, which is the physician's concern, nor property, which is the magistrate's, but the soul.
outliers: Ellicott alone concedes that the churches had met, taught, baptised and broken bread before any elders were appointed, and concludes that organisation of this kind was important for the permanence of the Church but not essential to its being.
Clarke alone reconstructs the history of the word from an old canonist, showing how a term that once meant counting raised hands at an election came to mean the bishop extending his hand in blessing.

Calvin alone reaches for a pagan proverb in commenting on tribulation, that it is best not to be born and next best to die very quickly, before setting against it the comfort that this hard way leads to the kingdom of heaven.
Wesley alone marvels at the raw material, that elders were made of men themselves newly converted, and takes it for proof that God can enable even a babe in Christ to build up others.

24.pericope_label: And after they had passed throughout Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia. And when they had preached the word in Perga, they went down into Attalia:

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the route and the silence about Attalia. Gill says that after they had passed throughout Pisidia, the country where Antioch, the last place mentioned, was, they came to Pamphylia. On the next verse he says Perga was a city in Pamphylia, and that the Alexandrian copy and others, and three manuscripts, read the word of the Lord, as do the Vulgate Latin and Syriac versions. They went down into Attalia, not Italy as some Latin copies and the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic versions read, but a city in Pamphylia bordering on the sea, Gill says; an old authority says that Attalia is a city of Pamphylia on the sea coast and was formerly the metropolis of it. It is now in the hands of the Turks and is called Sattalia, Gill adds, and near it is a bay called the Gulf of Sattalia, where there is a considerable mart for the whole country; it is famous for tapestry, which is made in it, and it had its name from Attalus, king of Pergamus, the first founder of it. An ancient copy here adds, preaching the Gospel to them, that is, to the inhabitants of Attalia, and doubtless with success, though no mention is made of it here, nor elsewhere, nor of any church in this place. Calvin says we have already said that Paul and Barnabas came to Antioch of Pisidia, and that, being now about to return to Antioch of Syria whence they were sent away, they go through Pamphylia, which is the middle region toward the mount Taurus; Perga and Attalia are cities lying near together. Whereas Luke saith that they preach the Word in the one only, Calvin says, we may thereby guess that they had not opportunity offered them everywhere to teach, which they were wont to neglect or let pass nowhere.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the places and the harbour. Barnes says they passed throughout Pisidia and came to Pamphylia, and that these places they had visited before. On the next verse he says Attalia was a city of Pamphylia situated on the sea shore, built by Attalus Philadelphus, king of Pergamus, who gave it his own name, and that it is now called Antali. Ellicott says the travellers retrace their steps, and that there is a coincidence more or less striking in the report of what they did at Perga: in the earlier chapter there is no mention of their having preached in that city, but we are simply told that Mark left them there and that they then went on to Antioch, so that on their return, accordingly, they did what they had then left undone. On their first journey they had gone straight from Paphos to Perga up the Cestrus, Ellicott says, and now they made a détour which led them to the port at the mouth of the Catarrhactes, named after Attalus Philadelphus, King of Pergamus. There is no record of any work done there, and they probably only went to it as the port where they were most likely to find a sailing-vessel that would take them to Antioch, Ellicott says; their ship would naturally pass between Cilicia and Cyprus, enter the Orontes at Seleucia, and sail up to Antioch. Robertson says they now stopped and preached in Perga, which they had apparently not done before, and that after leaving Antioch they passed on through Pisidia, as if Antioch was not strictly in Pisidia, and into Pamphylia. They crossed from Perga to Attaleia, the port of Perga, sixteen miles down the Cestrus and capital of Pamphylia, to find a ship for Antioch in Syria, Robertson says; it is now called Adala and for long was the chief harbour of the south coast of Asia Minor. We do not know why they did not revisit Cyprus, he adds, perhaps because no permanent Gentile churches were founded there.

Clarke and Wesley take the itinerary. Clarke says that when they had passed throughout Pisidia they came to Pamphylia, and that Attalia was a sea-port town there; thus we find the apostles travelled from Derbe to Lystra, from Lystra to Iconium, from Iconium to Antioch of Pisidia, from Antioch to Perga in Pamphylia, and from Perga to Attalia, and it appears that they travelled over three provinces of Asia Minor, Pamphylia, Lycaonia and Pisidia. Wesley says only that Perga and Attalia were cities of Pamphylia.

debates: Whether anything was preached at Attalia. Ellicott says there is no record of work done there and that they probably went only to find a ship for Antioch; Calvin infers from the Word being preached at Perga only that they had not opportunity everywhere, teaching being a thing they let pass nowhere; Gill reports an ancient copy which adds that they did preach the Gospel to the inhabitants, and doubtless with success, though no church there is heard of afterwards.

Where Attalia lay in relation to Perga. Robertson calls it the port of Perga, sixteen miles down the same river and the capital of Pamphylia; Ellicott calls the visit a détour to a harbour at the mouth of a different river, since the outward journey had gone straight up from the coast to Perga; Clarke and Barnes place it simply as a sea-port town of Pamphylia.

What the town is now called. Gill calls it Sattalia and describes the bay beside it, its mart and its tapestry; Barnes calls it Antali; Robertson calls it Adala and the chief harbour of the south coast of Asia Minor; the three names are the same place a century apart.

Why Perga is mentioned now and not before. Ellicott calls it a coincidence, that the outward chapter records only Mark's departure and on the return they did what they had left undone; Robertson says plainly that they now preached where they apparently had not preached before; Barnes says only that these were places they had visited before.
outliers: Robertson alone asks why Cyprus was not revisited on the way home, and suggests it was because no permanent Gentile churches had been founded there.

Gill alone follows the harbour into his own century, noting that it is in the hands of the Turks, that a considerable mart for the whole country is held in the bay beside it, and that the town is famous for its tapestry.
Clarke alone sets out the full return itinerary city by city and counts the provinces crossed.

26.pericope_label: And thence sailed to Antioch, from whence they had been recommended to the grace of God for the work which they fulfilled. And when they were come, and had gathered the church together, they rehearsed all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles. And there they abode long time with the disciples.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the commission, the credit and the door. Gill says they sailed thence to Antioch in Syria. On the next verse he says they were come to Antioch, and on the last that Paul and Barnabas continued a considerable time at Antioch with the believers there before they set out on another journey, and that what might detain them the longer might be the disputes they had with some judaizing Christians concerning the observation of the law, of which and of the issue of them an account is given in the next chapter. Calvin says Luke might have said that they were ordained there to be the apostles of the Gentiles, but by a circumlocution he doth more plainly express that they were neither sent away of men, neither did they attempt any thing trusting to their own strength, but that their whole journey, together with the success, was committed to God, the author thereof; therefore their preaching was no man's work, but a work of the grace of God. The word is referred as well unto the power and efficacy of the Spirit as unto all the rest of the signs of favour, Calvin says, because all those gifts be free which God bestoweth upon his servants, and the sentence may be resolved thus, that they prayed God that he would show forth his grace to further the labours of his servants. On the next verse Calvin says that as those who return from an embassage used to give an account of their acts, so Paul and Barnabas declared to the Church all the sum of their voyage, that it may thereby appear what good success they had and how faithfully they behaved themselves in their office, and also that they may exhort the faithful to give thanks to God, as the thing itself gave them ample materials. Therefore Luke saith not that they did extol the things which they themselves had done, but whatsoever things the Lord had done by them, Calvin says; and he presses the Greek preposition, which he renders with them rather than together with them, lest any unskilful man ascribe some part of the praise to Paul and Barnabas as if they had been partners with God in the work, whereas Luke doth rather make him the only author of all those famous facts which they had done. Luke addeth immediately after that the Lord had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles, Calvin says, for though they were sent unto the Gentiles, yet the novelty of the matter caused them to wonder not a little; and not only did the sudden change make the Jews astonished, but it was to them as it were a monster that impure men, aliens from the kingdom of God, should be mixed with the holy seed of Abraham, that they might both together make one and the same Church of God. They are now taught by the event itself that it was not for nothing that there were apostles sent to them. Moreover, it is said that the door of faith was set open to the Gentiles not only because the gospel was preached to them with the external voice, but because, being illuminated by the Spirit of God, they were called effectually unto the faith, Calvin says: the kingdom of heaven is indeed set open to us by the external preaching of the gospel, but no man entereth in save he to whom God reacheth out his hand, and no man draweth near unless he be drawn inwardly by the Spirit. Therefore Paul and Barnabas show and prove by the effect that their calling was approved and ratified by God, because the faith of the Gentiles was as it were a seal engraven by the hand of God to establish the same.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the fulfilled commission, the phrase about the door, and the long silence. Barnes says they had been recommended to the grace of God where they had been appointed to this missionary tour by the church, his favour and protection having been implored for them in their perilous undertaking. This shows conclusively, Barnes says, that they had accomplished fully the work which was originally contemplated, it being strictly a missionary tour among the Gentiles, an important and hazardous enterprise and the first in which the church formally engaged, which is why so much importance is attached to it and so faithful a record of it preserved; that the act by which they were set apart to this was not an ordination to the ministerial office but an appointment to a missionary tour; and that it was not an appointment to the apostleship, since Paul was an apostle before, by the express appointment of the Saviour, and Barnabas was never an apostle in the original and proper sense of the term, so that it was a designation to a temporary work now fulfilled. Barnes draws the further remarks that the work of missions early engaged the attention of Christians, that it is attended with danger, men now being no less hostile to the gospel than they were in Lystra and Iconium, that missionaries should be sustained by the prayers of the church, and that in the conduct of Paul and Barnabas missionaries have an example both in founding churches and in bearing their own trials. On the next verse Barnes says they related what had happened, their dangers and their success, because they had been sent out by the church and it was proper that they should give an account of their work, and because it furnished a suitable occasion of gratitude to God; all was traced to God, and to open the door of faith is to have furnished an opportunity of preaching the gospel to the Gentiles. On the last verse Barnes says how long they abode is not intimated, but we hear no more of them until the council at Jerusalem: if the transactions recorded in this chapter occurred, as is supposed, about the year forty-five or forty-six, and the council at Jerusalem assembled in fifty-one or fifty-three, then here is an interval of from five to eight years in which we have no account of them, and where they were or what was their employment in that interval the sacred historian has not informed us. It is certain, however, that Paul made several journeys of which we have no particular record in the New Testament, Barnes says, since he preached the gospel as far as Illyricum, and in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians there is an account of trials and persecutions of many of which we have no distinct record and which might have occurred during this interval; we may be certain that these holy men were not idle, and we may learn from their example to fill up our time with usefulness and to bear all persecutions without a murmur. Ellicott says two years or thereabouts had passed since their mission, during which interval little probably had been heard of them, and we can picture to ourselves the eagerness with which the Christians of Antioch would gather to listen to their report. The phrase about opening the door of faith unto the Gentiles is noticeable as the first occurrence, as far as the chronological order of the books of the New Testament is concerned, of a very characteristic phrase, Ellicott says: it would seem to have been a favourite metaphor of Paul's, and comes in here probably as a fragment from his speech. From this point of view it is interesting to note the recurrence of the phrase in the Revelation, he adds, both Paul and John, representing as they did different sections of the Church, agreeing in the thought that the door of the Father's house was now opened wider than it had ever been before, and that no man might shut it. On the last verse Ellicott says the words probably cover an interval of more than a year, during which it is reasonable to suppose that the preaching of the two Apostles drew together a large number of Gentile converts. Robertson says they sailed away to Antioch, having been gone some eighteen months, and that high and serious thoughts filled the hearts of these first returned missionaries as they neared home: the grace of God had been with them, they had fulfilled the work to which they had been set apart by the Holy Spirit with the prayers of the Antioch church, and they now had a wondrous story to tell. On the next verse he says it was the first missionary meeting in history, and that it was not hard to get the church together when the news spread that Paul and Barnabas had returned; the suitability of the Gospel to become the religion of the world had not before been put to the test, and doubtless many wise-acres had predicted failure, as they did for later missionaries. It was a long story, for they had many things to tell of God's dealings with them, God having been with them all the while as Jesus had said he would be, Robertson says. Three times in Paul's Epistles he employed the metaphor of a door, perhaps a reminiscence of the very language of Paul here; the Gentiles now, it was plain, could enter the kingdom of God through the door of faith, not by law or by circumcision or by heathen philosophy or mythology. On the last verse Robertson says they tarried no little time, and that it was a happy time of fellowship: the experiment entered upon by the church of Antioch was now a pronounced success, undertaken at the direct command of the Holy Spirit, and they had prayed for the absent missionaries and rejoiced at their signal success. There is no sign of jealousy on the part of Barnabas when Paul returns as the chief hero of the expedition, Robertson says; a new corner has been turned in the history of Christianity, and there is a new centre of Christian activity. What will Jerusalem think of the new developments at Antioch? Paul and Barnabas made no report to Jerusalem.

Clarke and Wesley take the voyage, the credit and the five silent years. Clarke says this was Antioch in Syria, and that to reach it by sea they were obliged to coast a part of the Mediterranean Sea, steering between Cyprus and Cilicia, though they might have gone the whole journey by land; the reader will recollect that it was from this Antioch they had been sent to preach the Gospel to the heathen in Asia Minor, and that they fulfilled that work. On the next verse Clarke says they gathered together the Church by which they had been sent on this very important and successful mission, and that they rehearsed all that God had done with them, not what they had done themselves but what God made them the instruments of working; and how God by his providence and grace had made a way for preaching Christ crucified among the heathen, and how the heathen had received that Gospel which, through faith in Christ Jesus, was able to save their souls. On the last verse Clarke says how long the apostles tarried here we cannot tell, but we hear no more of them till the council of Jerusalem, generally supposed to have been held in the year fifty-one; and if the transactions of this chapter took place in the year forty-six, as chronologers think, then there are five whole years of Paul's ministry, and that of other apostles, which Luke passes by in perfect silence. It is very likely that all this time Paul and Barnabas were employed in extending the work of God through the different provinces contiguous to Antioch, Clarke says, for Paul himself tells us that he preached the Gospel so far as Illyria. Many of the tribulations and perils through which the Apostle Paul passed are not mentioned by Luke, particularly those of which he himself speaks: he had been five times scourged by the Jews, thrice beaten by the Romans, thrice shipwrecked, a whole night and day in the deep, probably saving his life upon a plank, besides frequent journeyings and perils from his countrymen, from the heathen, from robbers, in the city, in the wilderness, in the sea, among false brethren; of none of these have we any circumstantial account, and probably most of them happened in the five years which elapsed between the apostles' return to Antioch and the council of Jerusalem. Clarke closes the chapter by observing how carefully the apostles considered the different circumstances of Jews and Gentiles in preaching, supporting their assertions to the former from the Law and the Prophets, whose authority was beyond appeal, while to the latter, who had no revelation, they drew the proof of their doctrine from the visible creation and demonstrated by plain reasoning the absurdity of idolatrous worship. Wesley says recommended to the grace, or favour, of God, for the work which they had fulfilled, shows the nature and design of that laying on of hands which was mentioned in the earlier chapter.

debates: How long the stay at Antioch lasted. Ellicott reckons the words probably cover an interval of more than a year; Barnes counts from the received dates and gets five to eight years of which we have no account, filling part of it with the journeys Paul mentions and Luke does not; Clarke settles on five whole years passed by in perfect silence and fills them with the scourgings, beatings and shipwrecks of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians; Gill offers instead a reason for the delay, the disputes with judaizing Christians which the next chapter reports; Robertson calls it simply a happy time of fellowship.

Whose language the door of faith is. Ellicott calls it the first occurrence in the chronological order of the books of a characteristic phrase of Paul's and thinks it a fragment from his speech; Robertson says the same from the other end, that Paul's three uses of the figure may be a reminiscence of the language used here; Calvin is interested not in whose phrase it is but in what it means, that the door is opened by effectual calling and not by the external preaching alone.

What the setting apart at the outset had been. Barnes says the fulfilment proves it was neither an ordination to the ministry nor an appointment to the apostleship, but a designation to a temporary work, Paul being an apostle already and Barnabas never one in the proper sense; Wesley draws the same conclusion in one sentence about the laying on of hands; Calvin reads the phrase as putting the whole journey and its success into God's hands rather than defining an office.

Who is to be credited with the work. Calvin presses the preposition, refusing any sense that would make Paul and Barnabas partners with God; Clarke says the same, that they rehearsed not what they had done but what God made them the instruments of working; Barnes says all was traced to God; Robertson notes that God had been with them all the while, as Jesus had promised.
outliers: Robertson alone reads the homecoming as a turning point in church politics, observing that a new centre of Christian activity had appeared and asking what Jerusalem would think of it, since Paul and Barnabas made no report there at all.
Robertson alone notices what did not happen, that Barnabas showed no sign of jealousy when Paul returned as the chief hero of the expedition.

Clarke alone closes the chapter with a comparison of method, that the apostles argued to Jews from the Law and the Prophets, whose authority was beyond appeal, and to Gentiles from the visible creation and plain reasoning about the absurdity of idols.

Ellicott alone follows the metaphor forward to the Revelation, so that Paul and John, representing different sections of the Church, are found agreeing that the door of the Father's house stood open wider than ever and that no man might shut it.
